HOMAGE TO MARTYRS OF THE QUIT INDIA MOVEMENT 
MR. CHAIRMAN: Hon. Members, today is the 63rd Anniversary of the 
historic day when the "Quit India Movement' was launched in 1942 under 
the leadership of Mahatma Gandhi. The whole nation responded to the 
clarion call of Gandhiji and participated in the Movement with single-minded 
commitment and dedication which culminated in our achieving 
Independence five years later. 
We pay our humble and respectful homage to all those martyrs who 
gave their lives, and also to those who suffered untold sufferings for the 
cause of our freedom. 
I would request hon. Members to rise in their places and observe silence 
as a mark of respect to the memory of martyrs. 
(Hon. Members then stood in silence for one minute)

WRITTEN ANSWERS TO STARRED QUESTIONS 
Pollution of underground water 
†*221. SHRI JANARDAN DWIVEDI: 
SHRI MOTILAL VORA: 
Will the Minister of WATER RESOURCES be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government's attention has been drawn to the report of the 
School of Environmental Sciences of Jawaharlal Nehru University which 
says that underground water is getting highly polluted due to a landfill 
arising in the form of hills in the Capital and in its bordering areas; 
(b) if so, the steps being taken by Government to curb this; 
(c) if not, the reasons therefor; and 
(d) the concrete arrangements being made by Government to check 
pollution of ground water and by when? 
THE MINISTER OF WATER RESOURCES (SHRI PRIYARANJAN 
DASMUNSI): (a) to (d) School of Enviro nmental Sciences, Jawaharlal Nehru 
University, New Delhi has carried out a study on ground water quality in 
†Original notice of the question was received in Hindi. 
4 

[9 August, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
vicinity of Bhalsava landfill site in Delhi. As per the study, ground water 
samples contains iron, manganese, copper, lead, nickel and zinc. The 
study has also indicated that the c oncentrations of metal increase as 
approached towards landfill. 
The Central Pollution Control Board (CPCB) has also carried out a 
study on heavy metal levels in ground water samples surrounding the 
Bhalsava landfill site. The studies have indicted presence of iron and zinc. 
However, samples collected have  shown signs of non-traceable 
concentration in respect of lead, chromium and cadmium. 
As per Municipal Solid Waste (Management and Handling) Rules, 2000, 
the local bodies are required to undertake improvement of existing landfill 
sites and design new landfill sites to protect ground water contamination. 
The Municipal Corporation of Delhi is in the process for setting up of new 
landfill facilities and also are contemplating to set up waste processing 
plant so that the burden on landfill for disposal of waste could be minimized. 
Optimum use of runways at Delhi and Mumbai airports 
*222.    SHRI V. HANUMANTHA RAO: 
SHRI B.K. HARIPRASAD: 
Will the Minister of CIVIL AVIATION be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that there are major delays for landings and 
take-offs at Delhi and Mumbai airports due to lack of runway space, etc.; 
(b) to what extent Government have been un-prepared for the expansion 
of air traffic; 
(c) whether Government will take the best advise possible to create 
immediate inter-mediate arrangements using the existing runway space; 
(d) whether it is a fact th at the Airports Authority of India has not used 
the latest methods to arrive at optimum use of existing runway and parking 
bay space at Mumbai and Delhi airports; and 
(e) the steps proposed to call in outside experts to devise new systems 
for use of runway space, etc? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE OF THE MINISTRY OF CIVIL AVIATION 
(SHRI PRAFUL PATEL): (a) and (b) Constraints are being experienced 
5 

RAJYA SABHA [9 August, 2005] 
during peak hours of traffic at De lhi and Mumbai airports on account of 
unprecedented increase in air traffic.  The development of infrastructure 
could not keep pace with the growth in traffic. 
(c) Yes, Sir. Airports Authority of India (AAI) has also taken initiatives to 
improve the infrastructure at Mumbai and Delhi like construction of parallel 
taxiways, high speed taxiways, additional parking bays etc. 
(d) The existing runway facilities at Delhi and Mumbai are being used 
near optimally to handle the flights within the given infrastructural 
constraints. AAI has also taken up co nstruction of additional parking bays 
on the space available at Delhi and Mumbai Airports. 
(e) A GIobal Technical Advisor has been engaged by AAI to assist in the 
process of restructuring of Delhi/Mumbai airports. Construction of second 
parallel runway at IGI Airport and additional taxiways have been included 
in the Mandatory Capital Projects to be undertaken by the Joint Venture 
Company (JVC) who will operate these airports after restructuring. 
Inflow of tourists in Madhya Pradesh 
†*223. SHRI P.K. MA HESHWARI: Will the Minister of TOURISM be 
pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government are aware that due to constant neglect of main 
tourist centres of Madhya Pradesh, there is continuous decrease in the

(b) if so, the details in this regard; 
(c) whether Government have any figures regarding the number of foreign 
tourists who visited Khajuraho during the last one year; and 
(d) if so, the details thereof? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE OF THE MINISTRY OF TOURISM (SHRIMATI 
RENUKA CHOWDHURY): (a) and (b) The State Government and the 
Central Government are committed to develop the Tourist locations of the 
State with a view to attracting more domestic and foreign tourists. As per 
the data provided by the State Government, 86,09,426 domestic tourists 
visited Madhya Pradesh during 2004 against 59,68,716 visits during 2003

showing an increase of 44%. Similarly, during 2004, 1,45,375 foreign 
tourists visited the State against 92,273 foreign tourists during 2003 showing

(c) and (d) As per the information received from the State Government,

Improvement in air traffic infrastructure 
*224. SHRI SHAHID SIDDIQUI: Will the Minister of CIVIL AVIATION 
be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that there is a shortage of ATC officers at most of 
the major airports, which is making our airports unsafe; 
(b) what steps have been taken to improve the infrastructure with 63 per 
cent increase in air traffic in the last five years; and 
(c) whether it is also a fact that due to  lack of area control centres there 
are gaps in the Indian skies and if so, what steps have been taken to 
remove these gaps? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE OF THE MINISTRY OF CIVIL AVIATION 
(SHRI PRAFUL PATEL): (a) There is some shortage of ATC officers at 
some airports. However, there is no compromise on safety as all the ATC 
units are manned by qualified Air Traffic Controllers and ICAO Standards 
and Recommended Procedures are being followed strictly. 
(b) Steps have been taken to provide additional ground infrastructure 
such as parallel taxiways, rapid exit taxiways and parking stands to 
enhance airside capacity at major airp orts. Additional air traffic routes 
through airport capacity (EMARSSH) project and Reduced Vertical 
Separation Minima (RVSM) have also been implemented to accommodate 
more number of aircraft in a defined airspace. Automatic Dependent System/ 
Controller Pilot Data Link Communication system has been installed at 
Kolkata, Chennai, Delhi and Mumbai airports. In addition, the Air Traffic 
Control facilities are also being regularly augmented through improvement 
of Communication, Navigation & Surveillance infrastructure, on the basis 
of the requisition received from user agencies so as to meet the growing 
air traffic requirements. 
7 

RAJYA SABHA [9 August, 2005] 
(c) There are 11 Area Control Centres (ACC) which are covering major 
portion of the Indian airspace. Some of the ACCs are not continguous and 
are independent of each other due to  the gaps in Very High Frequency 
(VHF) coverage and radar coverage. The gaps in VHF coverage is being 
covered by installing Remote Controlled Air Ground Communication 
(RCAGC) systems at various locations. Additional radars and radar 
networking are also planned. Besides, in collaboration with Indian Space 
Research Organization (ISRO), AAI is implementing GPS and GEO 
augmented Navigation (GAGAN), an augmentation system to enhance 
the accuracy and integrity of GPS sign als to meet precision requirements 
for providing augmentation service. A Dedicated Satellite Communication 
Network (DSCN) through Indian Satellite is also being installed so as to 
provide enhanced VHF coverage of Indian airspace through RCAG system. 
Five point agenda for improvement of investment climate 
*225.    SHRI JESUDASU SEELAM: 
DR. T. SUBBARAMI REDDY: 
Will the Minister of FINANCE be pleased to state: 
(a) whether World Bank has suggested a five point agenda for improving 
investment climate in India which includes easing restrictions on hiring 
and firing of workers and simplications of procedure for entry and exit of 
firms; 
(b) if so, what are the other points mentioned in the report; 
(c) whether Government have fully examined World Bank's five point 
programme to boost investment in India; and 
(d) if so, to what extent it has been implemented? 
THE MINISTER OF FINANCE (SHRI P. CHIDAMBARAM): (a) and (b) 
The World Bank in its annual report named "Doing Business in 2005" has 
used the following 7 indicators to benchmark regulatory environment in 
145 countries, including India. 
(i) Starting a business; 
(ii) Hiring and firing workers; 
(iii) Registering property; 
(iv) Getting credit; 
8 

[9 August, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
(v) Protecting investors; 
(vi) Enforcing contracts; and 
(vii) Closing a business. 
The report investigates the scope and manner of regulations that enhance 
business activity and those that constrain it. 
(c) and (d) Government have examined the report, particularly with 
reference to areas where procedures could be simplified to encourage the 
private sector within the country. Improvements in respect of the above 
indicators is an ongoing process. 
Rain Insurance Scheme 
†*226. PROF. R.B.S. VARMA: 
DR. CHHATTRAPAL SINGH LODHA: 
Will the Minister of FINANCE be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that Government have launched a Rain Insurance 
Scheme; 
(b) if so, the details of the same; and 
(c) the number of farmers likely to be benefited by this scheme during 
the current financial year? 
THE MINISTER OF FINANCE (SHRI P. CHIDAMBARAM): (a) and (b) 
The Agriculture Insurance Company of India Ltd. (AICL) has launched, 
during Kharif 2005, a rainfall based insurance product, namely Varsha 
Bima — 2005 in 130 districts spread over 10 states viz. Andhra Pradesh, 
Chhattisgarh, Gujarat, Karnataka, Ma dhya Pradesh, Maharashtra, Orissa, 
Tamil Nadu, Uttaranchal and Uttar Prad esh. The scheme covers anticipated 
shortfall in crop yield on account of deficit rainfall. It was voluntary for all 
classes of farmers. This scheme was available upto 15th June, 2005 for 
Sowing Failure option and upto 30th June, 2005 for Seasonal Rainfall 
Insurance/Rainfall Distribution Index. 
(c) AICL has reported that during Kharif 2005,1.25 lakh farmers were 
insured under the scheme with a sum insured of approx. Rs. 60 Crores.

Detection of adulterated cases 
†*227. SHRI NAND KISHORE YADAV: Will the Minister of PETROLEUM 
AND NATURAL GAS be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that the petrol and petroleum products are being 
adulterated with the nexus of the officers of the public sector undertakings; 
(b) if so, the reaction of Government thereto; and 
(c) the details of powers vested with these officers to stop adulteration 
and the number of cases of abuse of th ese powers reported during the last 
three years? 
THE MINISTER OF PETROLEUM AND NATURAL GAS (SHRI MANI 
SHANKAR AIYAR): (a) The Public Sector Oil Marketing Companies 
(OMCs) have reported that they have no established case of involvement 
of their officers in adulteration cases. 
(b) Does not arise in view of (a) above. However, there are Provisions 
under the Conduct Rules as also the Marketing Discipline Guidelines 
(MDG), 2005, to take action against offi cers found involved in irregularities/ 
malpractices, including adulteration. 
(c) The officers are empowered to inspect retail outlets, draw samples 
and send the samples to notified laboratories for testing. They are also 
empowered to carry out search and seizure under the provisions of various 
control orders issued under the Esse ntial Commodities Act. In case any 
irregularity/malpractice is established, action is initiated against the erring 
dealer under the MDG/Dealership Agreement. OMCs have reported that 
no case of abuse of these powers by their officers has been established 
during the last three years.

different rates to the gas consumers in the country; and

THE MINISTER OF PETROLEUM AND NATURAL GAS (SHRI MANI 
SHANKAR AIYAR): (a), (c) and (d) As per the extant policy for allocation 
and pricing of natural gas, effective from 1.7.2005, the consumer price 
of gas produced by ONGC and OIL from existing fields given to them 
on a nomination basis (APM gas) is Rs. 3,200 per thousand cubic 
metre exclusive of royalty, taxes and levies and transmission charges. 
The power and fertilizer sectors are critical to the economic 
development of the country and the output price of these sectors is 
either controlled or regulated by the Central and State Governments. 
Therefore, these Governments have to bear the burden of large subsidies 
in these sectors. Under court order, commitments have to be made to 
specific end users. Small scale consumers having allocations upto 0.05 
million standard cubic metres per day (MMSCMD) are also given priority 
in gas supply. Accordingly, it has been decided in the public interest 
that all available APM gas would be supplied to only power and fertilizer 
sector consumers against their existing allocations, in addition to the 
specific end users committed under Court orders and small-scale 
consumers having allocations upto 0.05 MMSCMD. However, the gas 
price for transport sector (CNG), Agra-Ferozabad small industries, and 
other small scale consumers, with allocations upto 0.05 MMSCMD, 
would be progressively increased over the next 3 to 5 years to reflect 
the market price. 
The price of gas for consumers ot her than those stated above is 
market related. 
(b) Under the Production Sharing Contract (PSC) regime, the 
company(ies) invest risk capital in a block for exploration of hydrocarbons. 
In case any commercial hydrocarbon discovery is made in the block, 
the contractor is required to share profit petroleum (which is determined 
after deducting eligible costs from revenues in accordance with the 
19 

RAJYA SABHA [9 August, 2005] 
provisions of the respective PSCs), based on either the Investment 
Multiple (IM) achieved under the PSC or in some cases on Post Tax 
Rate of Return (PTRR). The ratio or share of profit petroleum at various 
levels of IM is specified in the respective PSCs, and fixed on the basis 
of international competitive bidding at the time of award of the block. 
The Government share increases progr essively as the IM increases. IM 
is calculated on a cumulative basis and is a ratio of net revenue to investment 
(where investment includes all exploration costs and development costs).

Statement 
Outcome of the Studies conducted for Gujarat 
• "WADIS" spread over 25,000 acre on the private land of around 25,500 
families spread over 345 villages ha ve been established in two States 
i.e. Maharashtra and Gujarat. Thes e lands considered  as wastelands 
and non-productive assets,have become productive and sustainable 
assets. 
• Production has already started in Gujarat programme with 350 Mt. of 
cashew and over 500 Mt. of mango, which has been instrumental in 
establishing 10 village level processing units providing perennial 
employment to 180 landless tribal people, most of which are women. 
• Ten tribal co-operative societies have also been registered to facilitate 
the continuation of the programme once the external support is 
withdrawn. 
• The availability of protective irrigation through water resources 
development has increased cropping intensity. A shift in cropping pattern 
towards commercial crops such as vegetables and pulses has resulted 
in generating regular income. 
• The production of Vermicomposting and Nadep compost and emphasis 
on Bio-pesticides in the progra mme have opened up avenues for 
production of organically grown produce. 
• Seasonal migration has been reduced  to a great extent as "WADI" 
provides round the year employment opportunities to tribal families. There 
is a substantial rise in employment opportunities for landless in procuring 
and marketing of farm produce and processing of cashew and mango 
as well as other income generating activities in non-farm sector. 
• The health programme has reduced the incidences of infectious diseases 
in the area and has improved health and sanitation in the villages. 
• SHG movement has provided voice to tribal women and brought out their 
entrepreneurial skills which is dem onstrated by the micro enterprises 
and income generating activities such as nursery management, 
vermicomposting etc. undertaken by them. 
• The project was presented as a succe ssful replicable model for poverty 
alleviation in the developing countries at the UNDP Forum of ministers 
for Poverty and Environment in New York, USA in 1999 as well as at the 
global dialogue in Hannover, Germany. 
84 

[9 August, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
• The most striking contribution of the WADI programme is empowerment 
of the people to organize their affairs successfully. Though lack of basic 
infrastructural facilities like schools, banks, health centres, telephone, 
bus service etc., at village level, WADI has given way to many successful 
entrepreneurs in these remote villages.

Conclusions (Bached during seventh round table of Ministers-in-

IT enabled e-Governance 
1. It is recognized that IT (Information Technology and Communication) 
is a vital input of capacity for Panchayats so that they can perform their 
constitutionally and legislatively mandated functions better. 
2. IT ought to be primarily positioned as: 
(i)  a decision making support system for Panchayats themselves; 
(ii)   a fool for transparency, disclosure of information to citizens 
soeial audit; 
(iii)   a means for better and convergent delivery of services to 
citizens; 
(iv)   a means for improving internal management and efficency of 
Panchayats; 
(v)   a means for Capacity building of representatives and officials 
of the Panchayats. 
(vi)   an e-Procurement medium 
In this endeavour, the Round Table specifically proposes the following 
initiatives. 
95 

RAJYA SABHA [9 August, 2005] 
Process Re-engineering 
3. All States shall undertake a time-bound exercise of process re- 
engineering in consonance with the acitivity mapping already being 
undertaken by them for the functions transferred to the Panchayats, with 
a view to moving the processes of decision making, implementation, 
disclosure to the public, delivery of services and reporting and dissemination 
of information to Panchayat representatives to an IT enabled environment. 
4. In this exercise regard shall be had to avoid duplication of hardware 
and software initiatives by different  State Government departments and 
agencies. 
5. Considering the functional domain of Panchayats that potentially 
extends to 29 subject listed in the Eleventh Schedule, all e-Governance 
initiatives at the local level have to converge with the appropriate PRI as 
the nodal point. 
Data Ownership 
6. Such re-engineered processes sha ll ensure that the ownership of 
the data collected at the Panchayat level is with that level in the first 
instance, as the system becomes su stainable when those who use the 
data feel that they own it. 
7. While owning the data, the Panchayat could also operate, outsource 
or provide space to IT enabled multi service kiosk centers that provide IT 
enabled services to the people, including those that fall within the functions 
of the Panchayats. 
8. The Community Service Centers being rolled out by the Ministry of 
Information Technology at the Centre  may be located in the Panchayat 
offices so that panchayats services can also be delivered through these 
Common Services Centers (CSC). 
Training 
9. There has to be a systematic approach on training of staff and 
Panchayati Raj members through a cascading mode on use of IT. 
10. The opportunities offered by the satellite connectivity provided 
through the ISRO, including EDUSAT, can be used for undertaking training, 
96 

[9 August, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
11. While developing training material , regard shall be had to design 
user friendly approaches that can facilitiate training of the illiterate or the 
neo-literate. 
Software 
12. Development of common software application packages with provision 
for appropriate customization by states is preferred. In this connection, 
the National Informatics Centre (NIC), which being a government body 
present in all districts of the country and which has already done 
considerable software development for Panchayats, may be considered 
as the primary software provider. 
13. It is recommended that NIC strengthens themselves at all levels 
and provide dedicated staff through creating a Panchayat informatics 
divisions, with a time bound mandate to develop e-Govemance solutions 
to all levels of Panchayats. This will include the strengthening of the District 
Informatics Office of the NIC to support the District Planning Committee 
and the Panchayats. 
14. The National Panchayat Portal developed by the NIC for the Ministry 
of Panchayati Raj to become the information hub that links up Panchayats, 
the State Government and the Central Government for sharing of information, 
experiences and best practices. As a first step, all State Governments 
may immediately link and port the content of their existing Panchayat Raj 
websites or portals to the National Panchayat Portal and all District, 
Intermediate and Village Panchayats can be enabled and facilitated to 
link up with the portal. The content can be regularly updated by the respective .. 
stake holders. 
15. A repository of software solutions al ready developed by several states 
shall be maintained by the Ministry of Panchayat Raj or an institution 
nominated by it, so that they can be used by other states. 
16. Software development shall be pr imarily undertaken in open source 
software, with Indian language interphase, so as to reduce cost of replication 
and licencing. 
Hardware

for hardware and put in place a system  for transparent procurement through 
competitive bidding. '

1690. DR. MAM. RAMASWAMY: Will the Minister of PETROLEUM

has not been adequate to meet the demand of public; 
(b) if so, whether Government propose to direct the refineries to

THE MINISTER OF PETROLEUM AND NATURAL GAS (SHRI 
MANI SHANKAR AIYAR): (a) kerosene sold under the Public Distribution 
System (PDS) is an allocated product. In terms of the policy adopted 
124 

[9 August, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
by the Government of India, the allocation of PDS kerosene to various 
States/Union Territories was reduced  every year beginning 2001-02 till 
2004-05, taking into account the number of LPG connections released 
in each of the States/Union Territories. 
In view of the requests received from various State Governments for 
increasing the allocation, the Government of India have commissioned the 
first-ever detailed study of kerosene demand in the country, through the 
National Council of Applied Economic Research (NCAER) in December, 
2004. The final report of NCAER is expected by September, 2005. 
Pending the report of NCAER, and taking a view thereupon, for the year 
2005-06, allocations have been maintained at the level of 2004-05, including 
additional allocations made during that year to meet urgent demand of 
PDS kerosene in States/Union Territories. The decision about rationalizing 
the allocation of PDS kerosene among States/Union Territories would be 
taken after examining the NCAER report. 
(b) and (c) Although, current refinery capacity is sufficient to meet the 
domestic demand of PDS kerosene (SKO), Oil Marketing Companies who 
are distributing PDS kerosene had represented to Government that owing 
to non-availability of adequate quantities of SKO from domestic refineries, 
they have to import SKO at higher prices, whereas some of the stand- 
alone refineries were exporting Jet Kerosene/Aviation Turbine Fuel (ATF) 
which is equivalent to the PDS kerosene product. Considering that non- 
availability of kerosene may assu me significant proportions, it became 
essential that Government take pro-active action. Accordingly, a proposal 
to direct refineries to produce a minimum amount of kerosene have been 
examined. The Department of Legal Affairs have confirmed the powers of 
the Central Government to issue such an order under the Essential 
Commodities Act. In the meantime, Oil Marketing Companies have been 
advised to discuss the availability of kerosene with various refineries to 
meet domestic demand. 
The estimated requirement of PDS kerosene 2005-06 from refineries 
work out to approximately 7% of their estimated crude throughput for 2005- 
06 including private refineries.

Shortage of kerosene 
1691. SHRI T.S. BAJWA: Will th e Minister of PETROLEUM AND 
NATURAL GAS be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that shortage of kerosene oil is due to use of 
kerosene oil in automobile; 
(b) if so, the reasons therefor; and 
127 

RAJYA SABHA [9 August. 2005] 
(c) what steps Government are taking to prevent its commercial use? 
THE MINISTER OF PETROLEUM AND NATURAL GAS (SHRI 
MANI SHANKAR AIYAR): (a) to (c) Kerosene is sold as subsidized 
product 
through the PDS system, outside PDS allocations, there is free sale 
kerosene. PDS kerosene is allocated by the Government of India to the 
States/Union Territories. 
Government are aware of attempts by unscrupulous elements to 
divert PDS kerosene for adulterating transportation fuels. Such attempts 
are largely driven by the price difference between kerosene and 
transportation fuels. 
Punitive action against adulteration is taken by the Government/ 
Public Sector Oil Marketing Companies (OMCs) under the following 
provisions:— 
(i) In accordance with the Control Orders issued by the Government 
under the Essential Commodities Act, 1995, to prevent fuel 
adulteration, State Governments are empowered to take action 
against those indulging in adulteration. Government have 
repeatedly urged State Governments/Union Territory 
Administrations to step up inspections/surprise checks to ensure 
that adulteration related activities are minimized and to exercise 
vigil/conduct inspections at various private firms, factories, 
processing units etc., under their jurisdiction to identify the 
perpetrators of adulteration and take stringent action against 
them within the available legal framework. 
(ii) OMCs undertake regular and surp rise inspections of retail outlets 
and also take action under Marketing Discipline Guidelines (MDG) 
and Dealership Agreements agains t those indulging in adulteration 
and malpractices. MDG provide for penalty of termination of 
dealership in cases of adulteration being established. 
Besides the measures already in place, Government have approved 
an innovative pilot project of the Ministry of Petroleum & Natural Gas for 
radically revamping the PDS kerosene distribution network with the 
primary objective of ensuring that this heavily subsidized project is 
actually made available in the required quantities at subsidized prices 
to the intended beneficiaries; and, secondly, to thus cap, reverse and 
128 

[9 August, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
eventually eliminate the diversion of  PDS SKO for adulteration. The pilot 
project is to be implemented in 10% of the blocks of the country for a 
period of six months. Thereafter, the working of the scheme would be 
independently assessed and, based on the experience gained, 
Government will consider scaling up the scheme to cover the entire 
country. It is hoped this will lead to a significant breakthrough in the 
delivery of subsidized SKO to the entitled segments of society and thus 
contribute to the curbing of diversion for adulteration.

Amendment to include Tourism in the Concurrent List 
1704. DR. NARAYAN SINGH MANAK LAO: Will the Minister of 
TOURISM 
be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that tourism despite being a subject of national 
importance, does not figure out in any of the three lists viz. Union, State 
and Concurrent; 
(b) whether it is also a fact that the Department Related Parliamentary 
Committee on Tourism has recommende d amendment to include tourism 
in the Concurrent list; 
(c) if so, the steps taken so far and by when the amendment is likely to 
be made; and 
(d) the reasons for delay in this regard? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE OF THE MINISTRY OF TOURISM 
(SHRIMATI RENUKA CHOWDHURY): (a) The subject 'Tourism-, as such, 
does not figure in any of the three lists of the Seventh Schedule of the 
Constitution of India. However, individual subjects related to tourism like 
Pilgrimage; Visas; Airways; Carriage of  Passengers by railways, sea or air; 
Ancient and Historical Monuments; Archaeological Sites; Museums; 
Communications; Land; Fairs; Inns & Inn-keepers; Theatres; Taxes on 
luxuries; Shipping and Navigation etc. do appear in one or the other list. 
(b) Yes, Sir. 
(c) and (d) In view of the fact mat "tourism" is not a single entity but an 
amalgam of number of activities like accommodation, food & beverages, 
transportation, entertainment services, travel agencies, safety & security; 
etc. which are under the administrative control of different Ministries or 
States, and thus involve legal issues, the feasibility of placing "tourism" in 
the Concurrent List of the 7th Schedule of the Constitution of India has 
144 

[9 August, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
been referred to M/o Law & Justice fo r advice. Based on the advice received 
from Ministry of Law & Justice, further decision shall be taken. In view of 
this, it is not possible to indicate a time frame.

1727. SHRI RAJU PARMAR: W ill the Minister of WATER 
RESOURCES be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that inspite of sincere efforts by the Central 
Government, the States have not improved the quality of drinking water; 
(b) if so, the reasons therefor; 
(c) whether guideline issued by Government to the States in regard to 
routine analysis of samples for physico-chemicals and microbial quality 
are not being followed by States; and 
(d) if so, the steps taken by Government in this regard? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF WATER 
RESOURCES (SHRI JAY PRAKASH NARAYAN YADAV): (a) and (b) 
Rural drinking water supply is a State subject. Central Government assists the 
State Governments in implementation of rural drinking water supply 
schemes by providing technical and financial assistance through the 
Centrally Sponsored Accelerated Rura l Water Supply Programme (ARWSP) 
of Ministry of Rural Development, Department of Drinking Water Supply. 
85% of the rural drinking water supply schemes are based on ground- 
water sources. Problems due to chem ical contamination of ground water 
namely arsenic, fluoride, salinity and nitrate get aggravated due to various 
reasons like over-extraction of ground water for irrigation purposes, lack of 
recharge of aquifers due to recurrent droughts and anthropogenic pollution 
due to industrial waste etc. All the above reasons contribute to the 
deterioration of drinking water quality from ground water sources. 
(c) and (d) As reported by the Ministry of Rural Development, Department 
of Drinking Water Supply the guidelines issued by Government of India to 
States for routine analysis of samp les for physico-chemical and microbial 
quality are being followed by the States by and large.

Northwest, Southwest and West district s. Nitrate in excess of permissible

*244. DR. GYAN PRAKASH PILANIA: Will the Minister of HOME 
AFFAIRS be pleased to state:

up; 
(c) in the light of above statistics, which were the first five States, where rape 
scenario was most alarming; and 
(d) the steps Government intend to take to improve the situation? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HOME AFFAIRS (SHRI 
MANIKRAO GAVIT): (a) to (d) The total number of rape cases registered in India 
during 2004 and the number of rapes per lac of population, with State-wise breakup, is 
enclosed at Statement (See below) 
On the basis of rape cases registered, the five States with highest incidence of 
rape during 2004 were Madhya Pradesh, West Bengal, Uttar Pradesh, Maharashtra and 
Assam, while on the basis of the crime rate, the top five States during 2004 were 
Mizoram, Tripura, Madhya Pradesh, Chhattisgarh and Assam. 
'Public Order* and 'Police' as per the Seventh Schedule to the Constitution of 
India are State subjects and, as such, registration, investigation, detection and 
prevention of crime is primarily the responsibility of the State Governments. 
Further, the Government of India has been from time to time issuing advisories 
to the State 
5 

RAJYA SABHA [10 August, 2005] 
Governments to make concerted efforts to improve the administration of the criminal 
justice system and to take effective measures to control crimes against vulnerable 
sections including women and children. In an advisory sent to the State Governments in 
May, 2004, the following points have been re-emphasized: 
i. There should be no delay in registration of FIR in cases of crime against 
women. 
ii. Cases should be thoroughly investigated and charge-sheets filed within three 
months from the date of occurrence of crime, 
iii. Police officials charged with the responsibility of protecting women 
should be sensitized adequately, 
iv. Helpline numbers of the Crime Against Women cells should be exhibited 
prominently in hospitals/schools/colleges premises, and in other suitable 
places. 
v. Women Police Cells and exclusive women police stations may also be set up 
to cater especially to women, as needed. 
vi. Women police officials should be recruited widely in the State Police Force. 
vii. Institutional support should be provided to victims of violence, and 
viii. Proper counselling should be provided to victims of rape.

Liberalisation of Visa rules for foreign students 
† *251. SHRIMATI SAVITA SHARDA : Will the Minister of HOME 
AFFAIRS be pleased to state: 
(a) whether keeping in view the fact that foreign students are extremely 
impressed by the world class education system in India, Government have 
decided to liberalise the Visa rules for the foreign students; 
(b) if so, the details thereof; and 
(c) by when the said decision would be implemented alongwith the 
number of foreign students likely to be benefited as a result thereof? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HOME AFFAIRS 
(SHRI SHRI PRAKASH JAISWAL): (a) Yes, Sir. 
(b) The changes that have been effected in the Student Visa regime, inter 
alia, include removal of restriction on the number of the courses a foreign 
student may undertake, counting the periodicity of the visa with respect to 
duration from the new course or five years whichever is less, flexibility to 
change the course/Institution, enhancing the period of 'Provisional Student 
Visa' to six months to enable the foreign students to get admission in Indian 
Institutions, allowing the foreign student to complete the course even if he/she 
fails as long as the Institution allows him/her to carry on the studies, and 
delegation of powers to the State Governments/UT administration and FRROs 
to grant extension of stay to foreign students. 
(c) Necessary instructions have been issued on 21.6.2005 to all Indian 
Missions/Posts abroad and State Governments to bring in force the new 
Student Visa regime with immediate effect. This would cover all foreign 
students other than those from Pakistan, who are desirous to come to India 
for studies or undergoing studies in India at present.

(b) if so, the long term and the short term measures that are proposed to be 
taken to bridge the gap between the demand and the availability of electricity? 
THE MINISTER OF POWER (SHRI P.M. SAYEED): (a) The supply and 
distribution of electricity to the ultimate consumers including domestic/industrial 
and farmers in a State is the responsibility of the concerned State Government/State 
Power Utility which decides priority of power supply to various categories of consumers. 
There is an overall shortage of power in the country which varies from State to State. In 
order to optimize utilisation of available power, State Governments/Power Utilities regulate 
supply of power to its consumers by imposing power cuts/restrictions and resort to loan 
shedding from time to time depending on availability and requirement of power. 
The State-wise power supply position in the country for the period April-June, 
2005 and the details of notified power cuts on industries and power supply to 
agricultural sector for the month of June 2005 are enclosed in the Statement-I, II and 
III respectively. (See below) 
(b) The following short-term and long-term measures are being taken to bridge 
the gap between demand and supply of power: 
Short-term Measures: 
(i) Maximization of generation beyond the programme and increase in plant load 
factor of thermal power stations. 
(ii) Transfer of power from surplus regions to deficit regions for optimal 
utilization of available energy in the country leading to reduction shortages 
prevailing in different regions/States. 
(iii) Coordinated operation and maintenance of hydro/thermal/ nuclear gas 
turbine power stations in the regional power system to optimally utilize the 
existing generation capacity. 
(iv) Load management by way of imposition of statutory power cuts/ restrictions 
and load shedding by State Governments/Power Utilities from time to time 
depending upon the availability and requirement of power. 
(v) Redistribution of allocation of power from unallocated quota of Central 
generating stations.

(ix) Advising project authorities to incorporate incentiv e clause in the

(ii) Renovation and modernization and life extension of old and 
inefficient generating units through loans by Power Finance 
Corporation with interest subsidy. 
(iii) Strengthening/augmentation of sub-transmission and distribution 
systems through funds to the St ates under Accel erated Power

Rajiv Gandhi Grameen Vidyutikaran Yojana.

generation capacity and inter-regional transfer of power.

Review of the drinking water crisis 
*255. SHRI V. NARAYANASAMY: Will the Ministar of RURAL 
DEVELOPMENT be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government are planning to review drinking water crisis in the 
country; 
(b) whether Government are aware that the drinking water supplied in 
villages in some parts of the country is unfit for consumption; and 
(c) if so, what are the steps Government is planning to provide quality 
water in rural areas? 
THE MINISTER OF RURAL DEVELOPMENT (SHRI 
RAGHUVANSH PRASAD SINGH): (a) The primary responsibility of 
providing drinking water facilities in the country rests with State 
Governments. The Union Government has been extending policy, 
technological and financial support to the States in this endeavour through a 
Centrally sponsored scheme, namely  the Accelerated Rural Water S upply 
Programme (ARWSP). The Government of India regularly reviews the status of 
drinking water supply in all rural habitations of the country. As per the 
coverage status reported by the States, ou t of the 14.22 lakh rural habitations in 
the country included in the Comprehensive. Action Plan-1999, 13.67 lakh rural 
habitations have been fully covered and 50,479 habitations have been 
partially covered to provide the stipulated quantity of safe drinking water. As 
coverage status is a dynamic phenomenon, a fresh habitation survey was 
conducted in 2003 by the States, which is under validation by the Indian 
Institute of Public Administration, New Delhi. 
(b) As per water quality survey orde red in March, 2000 and conducted 
by the States, as on 31.3.2004, 2,16,968 rural habitations are affected with 
drinking water quality problems in terms of excess arsenic, fluoried, iron, 
salinity, nitrate or combination of these. 
(c) Drinking water supply is one of the six components of Bharat 
Nirman, which has been conceived as a plan for building rural infrastructure. 
The Plan, inter-alia, envisages to ensure provision of safe drinking water to 
remaining uncovered rural habitations and mitigating water quality problems 
and coverage of slipped back habitations.

impeding their development goals. In this regard, the need for tackling Non-Tariff Barriers

developing countries' interests and concerns must be fully reflected in the result of these

Negotiations for opening up of global farm goods market 
1767. SHRIMURLI DEORA: Will the Minister of COMMERCE AND 
INDUSTRY be pleased to state: 
(a) whether negotiations to open up the global farm goods market 
further, are not progressing satisfactorily and if so, the reasons therefor; 
(b) whether developed countries are primarily responsible for large 
distortions and protectiveness in the agricultural sector and if so, the details 
thereof; and 
64 

[10 August, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
(c) the steps taken to see that defensive concerns of developing 
countries in agriculture are addressed? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF COMMERCE 
AND INDUSTRY (SHRI E.V.K.S. ELANGOVAN): (a) Pursuant to the 
Framework Agreement on Agriculture of July 2004, negotiations have been 
proceeding on all the three pillars, namely, market access, domestic support and 
export competition, towards reaching agre ement on structural  aspects of the 
detailed modalities and further commitments by members of the World Trade 
Organisation (WTO). A broad understanding on the methodology for 
conversion of Non-Ad Valorem duties (NAVs) to their Ad Valorem 
Equivalents (AVEs) was reached in  May 2005, which is considered a 
prerequisite to the further negotiations on market access. It has also been 
broadly agreed that a Swiss formula would not be need for computing tariff 
reduction commitments. It has been agreed to intensify negotiations with a 
view to reaching agreement on the issues involved by the next Ministerial 
Meeting of the WTO scheduled for Hong Kong, China, in December 2005. 
(b) and (c) Reports by many eminent agri-economists and various bodies 
conducting research in agricultural policies of developed countries, including the 
World Bank, the International Monetary Fund and the Organisation of 
Economic Cooperation and Development (OECD), have concluded that high 
levels of protection, through combinations of tariff rate quotas, tariff peaks, 
tariff escalation, high specific duties, and subsidies, are prevalent on 
agricultural products in developed countries. Estimates of subsidies in OECD 
countries range between US$ 330 to 360 billion per annum, whose effect is to 
stimulate over production in high cost developed countries, to shut out 
potentially more competitive products from developing countries, and to 
distort trade in agricultural products. 
In order to redress this situation, in the on-going negotiations on 
agriculture in the WTO, India, along with other Members holding similar 
interests and concerns have demanded that, inter alia, all forms of export 
subsidies must be eliminated within a period of not more than five years, 
trade-distorting domestic support provid ed mainly by developed countries to 
their agriculture sector must be substantially reduced and substantial 
improvements in market access must be provided consistent with the mandate 
to negotiate agreed at the Doha 
65 

RAJYA SABHA [10 August, 2005] 
Ministerial Meeting of the WTO in November 2001 and the Framework 
Agreement of July 2004. Further more, special and differential treatment for 
developing countries must be integral to all aspects of the  negotiations, 
including through proportionately lower commitments and longer 
implementation periods for developing countries as compared to developed 
countries, and the negotiation of an appropriate tariff reduction formula that 
takes into account the different tariff structures of developed and developing 
Members. In order to safeguard their food and livelihood security and rural 
development needs, developing Members will be allowed to designate 
sensitive products and Special Products and a new Special Safeguard 
Mechanism to address any price depressions and surges in imports of 
agricultural products has also been  agreed whose details are under 
negotiation.

Provisions in the Armed Forces Special Powers Act (AFSPA) have been incorporated

insurgency. The Armed Forces are sensitized to ensure that no violation of human

violations by members of the Armed Forces in the North East. Out of 318 cases 
investigated, 290 allegations have been found to be baseless. In the remaining 28 
allegations, 63 Army personnel have been punished with penalties ranging from

1818. SHRI C. RAMACHANDRAI AH: Will the Minister of

THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF COMMERCE AND 
INDUSTRY (SHRI E.V.K.S. ELANGOVAN): (a) South Asian Free Trade Area 
Agreement (SAFTA) is scheduled to come into force with effect from 1.1.2006. Under 
SAFTA a phased tariff liberalization programme is envisaged. In 2 years, non-Least 
Developed Contracting States (India, Pakistan and Sri Lanka) will bring down tariffs 
to 20%, while Least Developed Contracting States (Bangladesh, Bhutan, Maldives and 
Nepal) will bring them down to 30%. Non-LDCS will then bring down tariffs from 20% to 
0-5% in 5 years, while LDCS will do so in 8 years. Moreover, non-LDCS will reduce 
their tariffs for LDC products on 0-5% in 3 years. 
103 

RAJYA SABHA [10 August, 2005] 
SAFTA is expected to be fully operationalized by 2016. A Committee of Experts on 
SAFTA (COE), consisting of delegates from all SAARC countries, is currently 
negotiating on the four outstanding issues pertaining to SAFTA, namely (1) Rules 
of Origin, (2) Sensitive List (3) Mechanism for Compensation of Revenue loss for the 
Least Developed Contracting States (LDCS) (MCRL) and (4) Technical Assistance to DCS 
(Technical Assistance) for finalizing the same for smooth implementation of SAFTA on 
the stipulated date. On the Indicative Sensitive Lists circulated by all SAARC 
countries, India has been holding bilateral discussions with each SAARC country, 
including Bangladesh and Pakistan, on the sidelines of the COE Meetings. 
(b) The existing bilateral trade agreements with Nepal and Bhutan will continue 
to be in force even after implementation of SAFTA. 
(c) Yes Sir. 
(d) The Ninth Meeting of the COE was held in Kathmandu on July 20-22,2005 in 
which delegates from all SAARC member countries participated which included delegates from 
India as well. The Committee held detailed discussions on all the four issues which are briefly 
indicated below: 
 
(1) SAFTA Rules of Origin—A proposal on Operational Certification Procedures 
(OCP) for smooth implementation of SAFTA Rules of Origin prepared by India 
was considered by the Sub-Group on the side lines of the Ninth COE Meeting 
and a substantial part of its text finalized. The COE urged the Sub-Group on 
SAFTA Rules of Origin to arrive at a consensus on outstanding issues with a 
view to finalizing the text of the DRAFT SAFTA Rules of Origin and 
Operational Certification Procedures at its next meeting. 
(2) Bilateral Negotiations on indicative sensitive lists—Bilateral negotiations 
were held during the Meeting on Sensitive Lists and agreed to finalize these at its 
Tenth Meeting. The COE reiterated its decision that each Member State would 
prepare one Sensitive list containing not more than 20% of Tariff lines at 6-digit 
for the purpose of negotiations with flexibility for Least Developed 
Member States to submit longer indicative lists; the final sensitive list of each 
Contracting State would comprise two lists i.e. one for LDC States and the 
other for Non-LDC States. 
104 

[10 August, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
(3) MCRL—Negotiations were held between the Non-Least Developed 
Contracting States and Least Developed Contracting States on the mechanism 
for compensation of revenue loss and it is expected to be further discussed 
during the next meeting of COE. 
(4) Technical Assistance—The Committee agreed that in the next meeting, the 
Sub-Group on Technical Assistance would finalize the operational modalities 
for providing technical assistance to LDCs.

electricity to ail areas and protecting interests of consumers and other 
stakeholders. 
2. Objectives: 
 
• Access to Electricity-Available for all households in next five years. 
• Availability of Power-Demand to be fully met by 2012. Energy and peaking 
shortages to be overcome and spinning reserve to be available. 
• Supply of Reliable and Quality Power of specified standards in an efficient 
manner and at reasonable rates. 
• Per capita availability of electricity to be increased to over 1000 units by 
2012. 
• Minimum lifeline consumption of 1 unit/household/day as a merit good by 
year 2012. 
• Financial Turnaround and Commercial Viability of Electricity Sector. 
• Protection of consumers' interests. 
 
3. CEA to notify first National Electricity Plan in six months with a perspective 
upto Twelfth Plan period. The Plan prepared by CEA to be used by prospective 
generating companies, transmission utilities and transmission/distribution 
licenses as reference document. 
4. Development of Rural Electrificati on Distribution backbone, village 
electrification and household electrification to achieve 
128 

[10 August, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
the NCMP target of completing household electrification in next five 
years. Financial support in terms of capital subsidy to States for rural 
electrification. Special preference to Dalit Bastis, Tribal Areas and 
other weaker sections for rural electrification. REC to be nodal 
agency for rural electrification at Central Government level. 
5. Creation adequate generation capacity with a spinning reserve of at 
least 5% by 2012 with availability of installed capacity at 85%. 
6. Full development of hydro potential. Provision of long tenor finance 
for these projects. 
7. Choice of fuel for thermal generation to be based on economics of 
generation and supply of electricity. 
8. Development of National Grid. 
9. Cost of recovery of service from  consumers at tariff reflecting 
efficient Costs to ensure financial viability of the sector. 
 
10. Provision of support to lifeline consumers (households below 
poverty line having consumption of 30 units per month) in terms of 
tariffs. 
11. Availability based tariff (ABT) to be extended to State level for 
better grid discipline through economic signaling. 
12. Special emphasis on time bound reduction of transmission and 
distribution losses. 
13. Measures to promote competition aimed at consumer benefits. 
14. Reliability and quality of power supply to be monitored by State 
Electricity Regulatory Commissions 
15. Exploitation of non-conventional energy sources such as small hydro, 
solar, biomass and wind for additional power generation capacity. 
Other Features 
16. Emphasis on achieving higher efficiency levels generating plants 
through necessary renovation and modernization. 
129 

RAJYA SABHA [10 August, 2005] 
17. Central Government to facilitate the continued development of national grid. 
CTU and STU to undertake coordinated planning and development. 
18. Transmission capacity to have redundancy level and margins as per 
international standards. 
19. Adequate transitional financial support for reforming power utilities. 
Encouragement for private sector participation in distribution. 
20. The State Regulatory Commissions to put in place independent third party 
meter testing arrangement. 
21. Support for adoption of IT system for ensuring correct billing to consumers. 
22. Speedy implementation of stringent measures against theft of electricity. 
23. Full emphasis on augmentation of R&D base. Mission approach for identified 
priority areas. 
24. Demand side management through energy conservation measures. Labels regarding 
energy efficiency to be displayed on appliances. Efficient agricultural pumpsets 
and efficient lighting technologies to be promoted. Appropriate tariff structure for 
managing the peak load. 
25. Special attention for developing training infrastructure in the field of 
regulation, trading and power market. 
26. For giving boost to renewable and non-conventional energy sources, a 
prescribed percentage of power, as specified by State Regulatory Commissions, 
to be purchased from such sources of energy at the earliest. 
27. Necessary regulations and appointing Ombudsman for redressal of consumers' 
grievances to be in place in six months.

Statement 
Salient Features of Rajiv Gandhi Grameen Vidyutikaran Yojana 
(Ministry of Power Office Memorandum No. 44/19/2004-D(RE) dated 
18th March, 2005) 
Sub: Rajiv Gandhi Grameen Vidyutikaran Yojana — Scheme of Rural 
Electricity Infrastructure and Household Electrification 
Approval of the President is convey ed for the "Rajiv Gandhi Grameen 
Vidyutikaran Yojana — Scheme of Rural Electricity infrastructure and 
Household Electrification" for the attainment of the National Common 
Minimum Programme (NCMP) goal of providing access to electricity to all 
households in five years. 
1. The scheme would be implemented through the Rural Electrification 
Corporation (REC). 
2. Ninety per cent capital subsidy would be provided for overall cost of 
the projects under the scheme. 
3. The present approval is for implem entation of Phase I of the scheme 
for capital subsidy of Rs. 5000 Crores during the Tenth Plan period. 
4. States must make adequate arrangements for supply of electricity and 
there should be no discrimination in the hours of supply between 
rural and urban households. 
5. For projects to be eligible for capital subsidy under the scheme, prior 
commitment of the States would also be obtained before sanction of 
projects under the scheme for: 
i.   deployment of franchisees for the management of rural 
distribution in projects financed under the scheme, and 
ii. the provision of requisite revenue subsidies to the State Utilities as 
required under the Electricity Act, 2003. 
6. Scope of the Scheme 
Under the scheme, projects could be financed with capital subsidy for 
provision of— 
136 

[10 August, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
6.1 Rural Electricity Dist ribution Backbone (REDB) 
- Provision of 33/11 KV (or 66/11 KV) sub-stations of adequate 
capacity and lines in blocks where these do not exist. 
6.2 Creation of Village Electrification Infrastructure (VEI) 
- Electrification of un-electrified villages. 
- Electrification of un-electrified habitations. 
- Provision of distribution transformers of appropriate capacity in 
electrified villages/habitation(s). 
6.3 Decentralised Distributed Generation (DDG) and Supply 
- Decentralised generation-cum-distribution from conventional 
sources for villages where grid connectivity is either not feasible or not 
cost effective provided it is not covered under the programme of Ministry 
of Non-conventional Energy Sources for providing electricity from non- 
conventional energy sources under their remote village electrification 
programme of 25000 villages. 
6.4 REDB, VEI and DDG would also  cater to the requirement of 
agriculture and other activities including 
• irrigation pumpsets 
• small and medium industries 
• khadi and village industries 
• cold chains 
• healthcare 
• education and IT 
This would facilitate overall rural development, employment 
generation and poverty alleviation. 
6.5 Rural Household Electrification of Below Poverty Line 
Households: 
Electrification of un-electrified Below Poverty Line (BPL) households 
would be financed with 100 Percent capital subsidy as per norms of 
137 

RAJYA SABHA [10 August, 2005] 
Kutir Jyoti Programme in all rural habitations. Households above poverty line 
would be paying for their connections at prescribed connection charges and 
no subsidy would be available for this purpose. 
The over-all subsidy of components from paras 7.1, 7.2, 7.3, 7.5 taken 
together should be kept within 90 percent of the overall project cost. The 
over-all cost estimate of different components for all villages and households 
are at the Statement-I. (See below). 
6.6 The project covers the entire country. The details of the un-electrified 
villages and households access to electricity as per census 2001 is in the 
Statement-ll and III. (See below). 
7. Franchisees:  
In the management of rural distribution through franchisees who could 
be Non-Governmental Organisations (NGOs), Users Association, Cooperatives 
or individual entrepreneurs, the Panchayat institutions would be associated. 
The franchisees arrangement could be for system beyond and including feeders 
from sub-station or from and including Distribution Transformer(s). 
8. Revenue Sustainability  
Based on the consumer mix and the prevailing consumer tariff and 
likely load, the Bulk Supply Tariff (BST) for the franchisee would be 
determined after ensuring commercial viability of the franchisee. Wherever 
feasible, bidding may be attempted for determining the BST. The Bulk Supply 
Tariff would be fully factored into the submissions of the State Utilities to the 
State Electricity Regulatory Commi ssions (SERCs) for their revenue 
requirements and tariff determination. The State Government under the 
Electricity Act is required to provide the requisite revenue subsidies to the 
State Utilities if it would like tariff for any category of consumers to be lower 
that the tariff determined by the SERC. While administering the scheme, prior 
commitments may be taken from the State Government regarding— 
a) Determination of Bulk Supply Tariff for franchisees in a manner 
that ensures their commercial viability. 
b) Provision of requisite revenue subsidy by the State 
Government to the State Utilities as required under the Electricity Act. 
138 

[10 August, 2005] RAJYA  SABHA 
9. The capital subsidy for eligible projects under the scheme would be 
given through REC. These eligible projects shall be implemented 
fulfilling the conditionalities indicated above. In the event the projects 
are not implemented satisfactorily in accordance with the 
conditionalities indicated above, the capital subsidy could be 
converted into interest bearing loans. 
10. The services of Central Public Sector Undertakings (CPSUs) have 
been offered to the States for assisting them in the execution of Rural 
Electrification Projects as per their willingness and requirement. With 
a view to augment the implementation capacities for the programme, 
REC has entered into Memorandum of Understanding (MOU) with 
NTPC, POWERGRID, NHPC AND DVC to make available CPSUs' 
project management expertise and capabilities to States wishing to use 
their services. This is being operationalised through a suitable 
Tripartite Agreement. 
11. Upto 1 percent  of the total subsidy under  the scheme would be used 
for associated works/ef forts of the programme linked to research, 
technology development, capacity building, information system 
development, awareness and other administrative and associated 
expenses and undertaking of pilot studies and projects 
complimentary to this rural electrification scheme. 
12. This scheme merges the existing "Accelerated Electrification of one 
lakh Villages and one crore Households" and the Minimum Needs 
Programme for rural electrification. 
13. The scheme will be subject to evaluation and a view on modification 
required for implementation during Eleventh Plan will be taken after 
a comprehensive review towards the end of Tenth Plan. 
14. The expenditure involved on above scheme would be debitable to the 
following Head under Grant No. 73 —Ministry of Power for the year

Deficit of Power 
1853. SHRI B.J. PANDA: Will the Minister of POWER be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government are aware that some of our States are in the grip of a 
severe power crisis where the power deficit ranges from 7 per cent to 25 per cent in 
April, 2005; 
(b) whether Government are also aware that the deficit of power is adversely 
affecting not only industrial/agriculture sector but also hard-hitting the common 
man; 
(c) whether the major cause of the shortage is its theft, leakage, transmission 
and commercial losses; and 
(d) if so, the action plan of Government to address these issues? 
THE MINISTER OF POWER (SHRI P.M. SAYEED): (a) and (b) The energy 
deficit in April, 2005 varied from 7% to 25% in the States like J&K and Uttar Pradesh in 
Northern Region; Madhya Pradesh, Gujarat and Maharashtra in Western Region; Bihar in 
Eastern; Assam, Manipur, Meghalaya, Mizoram, Nagaland and Tripura in North Eastern 
Region. State-wise power supply position in the country for the month of April, 2005 
is given in the Statement. (See below). 
The supply and distribution of electricity to the ultimate consumers including 
domestic/industrial and farmers in a State is the responsibility of the concerned State  
Government/State Power Utility/Distribution 
147 

RAJYA SABHA [10 August, 2005] 
Agency. There is an overall shortage of power in the country which varies from State to 
State. In order to optimize utilisation of available power, power cuts/restrictions and 
load shedding are imposed by State Governments/State Power Utilities/Distribution 
Agencies from time to time so that the requirement of agricultural sector, supply to 
essential consumers and minimum requirement of core sector industries are 
adequately met. 
(c) and (d) There are a number of reasons for shortage of power including 
growth in demand for power outstripping the growth in generation and capacity 
addition, shortage of peaking power, low Plant Load Factor of thermal generating 
units mainly in the State sector, inadequate sub-transmission and distribution network 
in some States, high Transmission and Distribution losses, theft of power, poor financial 
position of States/Utilities rendering it difficult for them to raise the resources 
necessary for making required investments to create adequate additional generation, 
transmission and distribution capacity, etc. Theft of electricity causes commercial loss to 
the States/Power Utilities whereas leakage and losses in transmission and distribution 
system reduce the availability of power. 
The following measures have been taken/are proposed to be taken to address the issue 
of theft, leakage, transmission and commercial losses: 
(i) The Electricity Act, 2003 has been enacted and implemented with effect from 
10th June, 2003 under which the provisions relating to theft are made 
more stringent. 
(ii)     Compounding of theft cases. 
(iii)     Adoption of High Voltage Di stribution System (HVDS) in theft prone 
areas and rural areas. 
(iv)     Replacement of defective meters and installation of meters for all 
consumers. 
(v)     Replacement of LT overhead lines by insulated aerial bunched conductors 
(ABC), to stop power theft by direct hooking of lines. 
(vi)    Carrying out Energy Accounting and Audit. 
(vii)     Introduction of Information Technology (IT) in billing, collection and 
revenue realization.

Government of India with the State Government informing it that NHPC would also 
file a review petition in the Hon'ble Supreme Court for modification of its order dated

† 1867. SHRIMATI KAMLA MANHAR: Will the Minister of RURAL 
DEVELOPMENT be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government have formulated any plan to give assistance to 
the States suffering from potable water crisis; 
(b) whether it is also a fact that Government have prepared any outline for 
giving special economic assistance to the major States suffering from potable water 
crisis by giving special category status to such States to save them from this crisis

thereof?

DEVELOPMENT (SHRI A. NARENDRA): (a) to (c) A Centrally sponsored scheme, 
namely Accelerated Rural Water Supply Programme (ARWSP), already exists to provide 
financial assistance to the States for providing drinking water facilities in rural habitations.

into account the rural population, geo-hydrological conditions, number of not covered/ 
partially covered habitations and water quality situation in the State/UT. State 
Governments/UT Administrations can utilize 15% of the allocated funds for tackling 
water quality problem. Recently, the Government of India has conceived Bharat 
Nirman plan for development of rural infrastructure in four years. Drinking Water 
Supply is one of the six components of Bharat Nirman, which envisages, inter-alia, 
tackling of water quality problems in all quality-affected habitations. There is, 
however, no proposal under consideration to give special category status to any of the 
States.

2,52,682 hectares since 1.4.1995. A total of Rs. 50.45 crores have been 
released from 1.4.1995 till date to the State. Zilla Panchayat is the nodal agency 
for implementation of the programme in the State. In the current financial 
year, 15 new projects for treatment of an area of 70000 ha. at a total cost of Rs. 
42.00 crores have been sanctioned to the State and first instalment of Central 
share amounting to Rs. 5.775 crores for these projects has been released to the 
concerned Zilla Panchayats. Total funds released including on-going projects 
during the year 2005-06 amounts to Rs. 9.069 Crores so far. Areas not 
identified as DPAP blocks in the State are eligible for IWDP projects. 
(b) The impact assessment studies  conducted and the mid-term 
evaluation reports of ongoing projects in the State of Chhattisgarh show that the 
net sown area and area sown more than once have increased in project areas. 
Water table levels are also reported to have increased by 1 to 2 meters in 74% 
of the wells in the watershed areas. Water harvesting structures and water 
bodies created in the project areas have substantially increased the irrigation 
potential. Nearly 70% of the respondents (both beneficiaries and non-
beneficiaries) reported an increase in fuel wood and fodder availability following 
the implementation of the programme. Income generating capacity has increased 
as a result of vocational trainings being imparted to the stack-holders. Out 
migration of the job seekers from project areas has substantially reduced.

Initiatives to boost textile exports 
1880. DR. KARAN SINGH: 
DR. T. SUBBARAMI REDDY: 
Will the Minister of TEXTILES be pleased to state: 
(a) whether the current row between China on one hand and United States 
and the European Union on the other is likely to help Indian textile exports; 
(b) if so, whether the recent initiatives taken by Government and 
manufacturers will also help boost exports; 
(c) whether US and EU have imposed an import quota on Chinese 
products according to the provision of the Textile specific Measures clause of 
the Accession Agreement signed by China; and 
(d) if so, to what extent this quality fixation has helped India to 
improve its trade with US and EU? 
THE MINISTER OF TEXTILES (SHRI SHANKERSINHVAGHELA): 
(a) to (d) As per the agreement reached between EU and China on 10th June, 
2005, EU has limited the growth of Chinese textiles exports to Europe in 10 
product categories under caps ranging from 8% to 12.5% per year. The actual 
growth rates of these categories of products during January - March 2005 over 
the corresponding period January - March 2004 range from 51 % to 534% 
depending on the category. Thus the growth rate has been severely restricted in order 
to give a period of adjustment for the EU textile industry to adjust after the 
elimination of the quota system. This agreement will expire in 2007. India is a 
major exporter in most of the product categories affected by the Agreement, 
while we are a leading exporter only in one category, table & kitchen linen. 
183

The restrictions placed by EU on Ch ina coupled with recent initiatives 
taken by the Government to boost exports  may help increase India's textile 
exports. 
US has also initiated proceedings under 'China Textile Safeguards' 
provisions on certain product categorie s originating from China. However, 
bilateral discussions between US and China have not been held so far. 
It is too early to make any realistic assessment about the increase in 
India's textile exports due to EU/US safeguards action against China.

Road link to Myanmar 
*261. SHRI MATILAL SARKAR: Wi ll the Minister of EXTERNAL 
AFFAIRS be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government are contemplating to take initiative in extending road-links 
to Myanmar across the North-Eastern States according to the 'look east' policy; 
(b) if so, the response received from other countries; and 
(c) if not, whether any other similar programme is being contemplated? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF EXTERNAL AFFAIRS 
(SHRI E. AHAMMED): (a) to (c) Government of India is undertaking a variety 
of cross-border projects with a view to improving connectivity 
 
1

RAJYA SABHA [11 August, 2005] 
between the North-Eastern States of India and Myanmar. Expansion of road 
links between the two countries constitutes an important aspect of these 
initiatives. 
In 2001, Government of India upgraded the 160 km. long Tamu-Kalewa-
Kalemyo in Myanmar which links India and Myanmar through the Tamu-Moreh 
(Manipur) border point. The Tamu-Kalewa-Kalemyo road was used during the 
first India-ASEAN car rally flagged off by the Prime Minister from Gawahati 
in November 2004. In addition, Government of India is committed to 
improving road connectivity at Zowkhathar (Mizoram)-Rhi, the second border 
trade point along the India-Myanmar border, by upgrading the Rhi-Tidm and Rhi-
Falam roads in Myanmar. 
Discussions are also underway for building a Trilateral Highway from 
Moreh in Manipur to Mae Sot in Thailand via Bagan in Myanmar. This 
would provide connectivity to North-East India up to Thailand and beyond to 
other ASEAN countries. 
Further, the Kaladan Multi-modal transport project which is expected to be 
implemented soon seeks to connect Indi an ports on the eastern coast with 
Mizoram through a combination of sea, inland waterway and highway 
connections. The highway component of the project would connect Kaletwa in 
Myanmar with the National Highway 54 at Nalkawn in Mizoram. 
The Myanmar Government has been cooperating with India on the above road 
projects. Thailand, which is involved in the Trilateral Highway project, is also 
keen to implement it.

Impact of tsunami 
*264. SHRI JANARDHANA POOJARY:  Will the Minister of OCEAN 
DEVELOPMENT be pleased to state: 
(a) whether any scientific analysis has been carried out for ascertaining the 
impact and havoc brought by the recent tsunami in the country; 
(b) if so, the details in this regard; 
(c) the measures that are contemplated to forecast tsunami and such other 
disasters in future and to meet the cha llenges thrown by such disasters in the 
future; 
(d) whether experts have suggested creating mangroves on the shores to 
minimize the impact of tsunami; and 
(e) if so, the details in this regard and Government's reaction thereto? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE OF THE DEPARTMENT OF OCEAN 
DEVELOPMENT (SHRI KAPIL SIBAL): (a) and (b) Yes Sir. A total of 2260 
line km. of coastal length was impacted by the 26th December, 2004 tsunami 
which included the entire coast of Andaman and Nicobar Islands and parts of 
Tamil Nadu, Andhra Pradesh, Kerala & Pondicherry. An estimated 12407 
human lives were lost. Estimated loss in monetary terms including damage to 
property amounts to Rs. 11544 Crores. 
Preliminary scientific assessment of the impact of tsunami has been 
conducted by various institutions and Government Departments on 
infrastructure and environment in the coastal areas of Andaman and Nicobar Islands, 
parts of Tamil Nadu, Kerala and Andhra  Pradesh. The Department of Ocean 
Development's vessels ORV Sagar Ka nya and FORV Sagar Sampada were 
deployed for studying the impact of tsunami on ocean environment and its 
resources in the Bay of Bengal and Arabian Sea during January—February 2005. 
The multi disciplinary and multi parameter data collection was so planned as to 
cover areas for which pre-tsunami data was available and also to collect new 
data in new areas. 
6 

[11 August, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
The tsunami waves have caused changes in the biological community of the 
coastal areas by transporting biological organisms from one area to other area 
along the same coast. These changes are likely to be short-term. The coral 
reefs of South Andaman Islands have been found to be damaged and covered 
with debris, mud and sand. There has been no significant impact on demersal 
fisheries. Coastal water quality investigations have indicated enrichment of 
nutrients and contamination by bacteria in the near shore waters of Tamil 
Nadu. Reverse trend was observed for water quality along Kerala Coast. 
(c) It has been proposed to set up a Tsunami and Storm Surge Early 
Warning system with the following components: 
• Strengthening of the existing seismological network to indicate in near 
real time occurrence of tsunamigenic earthquakes. 
• Installation of tsunami warning sensors close to the ocean bottom at 
appropriate locales in the Indian Ocean, with real time connectivity. 
• Tide gauge and data buoys networking to validate arrival of tsunami waves 
at the coast. 
• Modelling of the inundation scenarios for the entire coast and 
mapping of potential risk areas. 
• The establishment of a centre for collection of information, analysis and 
generating status advisories. 
The warning system is scheduled to be operational by September 2007. 
The system will require 10-12 Bottom Pressure Recorders (BPR) close to the 
ocean bottom w ith complementary floating data buoys with real time 
connectivity. Tide gauge networking has already been initiated and six of these 
with real time connectivity have been operationalised so far. The specifications 
of BPR and data buoys have been finalized. 
(d) and (e) the experts have suggested creation of bio-shield with 
appropriate vegetation including mangroves along the coast to minimise 
the impacts of tsunami. Under the mangrove Management Action Plan of 
the Ministry of Environment and Forests, 35 mangrove areas in the country 
have been identified for intensive conservation and management. 
7

media during his visit to Islamabad in June, 2005 that Pakistan Information 
Minister is the person in-charge of  terrorist training camps across our 
international border;

Yasin Malik had told the media, at a meeting during an exhibition in
