Ban on technology and materials 
1885. SHRI B.K. HARIPRASAD: W ill the Minister of EXTERNAL 
AFFAIRS be pleased to state: 
(a) whether India's inability to expand its present nuclear power generation 
capacity, which cover only 3 per cent of our total requirements is due to 
inadequate supplies of uranium and technological assistance coupled with embargo 
by a cartel called Nuclear Suppliers Group (NSG); 
(b) whether the NSG operates a blanket ban on technology and materials trade 
with black-listed countries, including India; and 
(c) If so, whether US has offered civilian nuclear energy cooperation with India 
which could lead the NSG to reconsider the ban currently in force? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF EXTERNAL AFFAIRS 
(SHRI RAO INDERJIT SINGH): (a) and (b) No, Sir. India has formulated a 
comprehensive indigenous three-stage nuclear power programme to expand its 
nuclear power generating capacity to 20,000 MW by the year 2020. 
International cooperation can supplement our indigenous efforts. However at 
present the Nuclear Suppliers' Group (NSG) guidelines prevent trade in nuclear 
technology and materials with India. According to these guidelines such items can 
be supplied to a non-nuclear-weapon State only when that State has brought into 
force an agreement with the IAEA requiring the application of safeguards on 
all its current and future peaceful activities. 
(c) The Joint Statement issued during the recent visit of Prime Minister to the 
US, states inter-alia "the United States will work with friends and allies to 
adjust international regimes to enable full civil nuclear energy cooperation and 
trade with India, including but not limited to expeditious consideration of fuel 
supplies for safeguarded nuclear reactors at Tarapur. In the meantime, the United 
States will encourage its partners to also consider this request epeditiously". 
Accident in CCL mine in Hazaribagh 
1886. SHRI LALIT SURI: 
SHRI DARA SINGH CHAUHAN: 
Will the PRIME MINISTER be pleased to state: 
(a) whether a number of workers got trapped inside the Central Coal Fields 
Ltd. (CCL) Saunda mine in Hazaribagh on the 14th June, 2005; 
32 

[11 August, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
(b) the number, out of them, who lost their lives and those who could be 
rescued; 
(c) whether the cause of the accident has been investigated; if so, the findings 
thereof and the action taken thereon; 
(d) the steps taken/proposed to be taken to prevent such mishaps; and 
(e) the nature of assistance givea to the families of those who lost their lives 
in the mishap? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF COAL (DR. DASARI 
NARAYAN RAO): (a) and (b) As per information received from Coal India 
Limited (CIL), at the end of the third shift of 14.6.2005, i.e. the morning of 
15.6.2005, fourteen employees (12 workmen and 25tipervisors) did not come 
out of Old Bansgara Incline of Central Saunda Colliery of Central Coalfields 
Ltd. (CCL), in Hazaribagh district, Jharkhand. The rescue and recovery 
operations along with action to de water the drawned area were taken 
immediately. Services of Naval divers for rescue of survivors were also utilized, 
but the precious lives of all the above 14 persons, who were trapped inside the 
mine, could not be saved. 
(c) The Directorate General of Mines Safety (DGMS) under the Ministry of 
Labour, which is the statutory body for enforcement of safety statutes in mines in 
the country, is conducting enquiry, under the Mines Act, 1952, into the 
accident. The enquiry is stated to be in progress. 
Besides, Ministry of Coal had constituted a committee under chairmanship 
of Chairman-cum-Managing Director, Central Mine Planning and Degine 
Institute Limited for holding a Departmental enquiry. The Committee has 
since submitted its report, which is under consideration. The main findings of 
the report are as under. 
(i) The accident was caused by fall of a large area of standing roof in the 
decoaled area leading to air blast. The presence of weak zone of strata 
might have contributed to the fall of roof which also resulted in inrush of 
water through the caved area from the water logged old workings of 
overlying seam. Ineffective dewatering of the overlying seam before and 
during depillaring is the major cause for this inundation. 
33 

RAJYA SABHA [11 August, 2005] 
(ii) Acts of negligence and dereliction of duty have taken place on the part 
of CCL officials. 
(d) To prevent such mishaps and to improve the status of safety in 
mines, following steps are being taken by the coal companies:— 
• Thurst on training and retaining of workmen, supervisors and 
managers to increase safety awareness. 
• Issue of guidelines for safer opera tions in identified thrust areas 
through circulars. 
• Promoting participation of workers in safety management. 
• Promoting self-regulation by management. 
• Tri-partite and Bi-partite review of safety status at various levels. 
• Observance of safety week and safety campaigns. 
• Generating safety awareness and information dissemination. 
• National Conference on Safety in Mines. 
• National Safety Awards. 
• Interactions at different forums with a view to promote safety, health and 
welfare of persons employed in mines. 
• Introduction to the concept of Risk Assessment, preparation of Safety 
Management Plan and Development of Emergency Response System. 
• Facilitating introduction of new technology in mining with low 
potential risk. 
(e) As reported by CIL, apart from compensation payable under the 
Workmen's Compensation Act, ex-gratia, life-cover, gratuity, leave 
encashment, benevolent fund, employment to one dependant of the 
deceased have been given. The amount of compensation paid to the affected 
families varies from Rs. 5.32 lakhs  to Rs. 6.86 lakhs depending upon the 
age and length of service of the d eceased persons. In addition to the 
above, kin of each deceased will be paid by Insurance Company against 
group insurance accident scheme which will be about Rs. 5 lakhs. Provident

Parity in procurement of equipment 
1913. SHRI V. NA RAYANASAMY : Will the Minister of 
COMMUNICATIONS AND INFORMATION TECHNOLOGY be pleased to 
state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that BSNL is demanding for parity in procurement of 
equipment with private telecom operators; and 
(b) if so, Government's reaction in this regard? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF COMMUNICATIONS 
AND INFORMATION TECHNOLOGY (DR. SHAKEEL AHMAD): (a) Given 
the nature of public and private sectors, there cannot be an absolute parity between 
them in the matter of procurement. While BSNL has not demanded any parity in 
procurement of equipment with private telecom operators, its concern was in 
respect of the proposed initiative of promoting indigenous telecom 
manufacturing in its procurements.

the objective, inter alia, of the availability of desired quality/standard products at 
competitive rates, immediate availability of after-sales services and development 
of new technologies in the Country. A procurement framework, whereby only 
vendors who indigenously manufacture (or have definite plans to do so) certain 
telecom products are alone eligible" for procurement is under active 
consideration by BSNL and MTNL.

National warning system for Tsunami 
1968. DR. VI JAY MALLYA: Will the Minister of OCEAN DEVELOPMENT

(a) whether Hyderabad based Department of Ocean Development (DOD) is 
setting up a long-term and round-the clock National Tsunami warning system;

centres? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE OF THE DEPARTMENT OF OCEAN 
DEVELOPMENT (SHRI KAPIL SIBAL): (a) to (c) It is proposed to set up a 
Tsunami and Storm Surge Early Warning system by the Department of Ocean 
Development with its Centre at the Indian National Centre for Ocean Information 
Services (INCOIS), Hyderabad. The system will comprise of the following 
components: 
• Strengthening of the existing seismological network to indicate in near 
real time occurrence of tsunamigenic earthquakes.

• Modelling of the inundation scenarios for the entire coast. 
• Collection of information, analysis and generating status advisories. 
The Centre is proposed to operate on round the clock basis.

Will the PRIME MINISTER be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Prime Minister on the conclusion of two days' National 
Development Council meet decided to constitute two NDC Sub-Committees on 
farming and State debts to devise ways to give a fillip to the overall economic 
growth; 
(b) if so, whether these two Sub-Committees were Constituted under the 
Chairmenship of Agriculture and Finance Minister; 
(c) if so, whether these two Committees would submit their report in a very 
short time and after receiving reports, the Planning Commission would include 
them in the approach paper of the Eleventh Five Year Plan; and 
(d) if so, the details of the reports made by these two groups? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF PLANNING (SHRI 
M.V. RAJASEKHARAN): (a) and (b) The NDC agreed to form a Sub-
Committee under Minister of Agriculture for drawing up implementable 
action plans in agriculture and related issues. It was also decided that a 
Committee will be set up separately under the Finance Minister to examine 
relevant issues relating to the debt burden of States and debt relief with 
reference to their debt outstanding against the National Small Saving Fund 
(NSSF). 
(c) The Committees will be requested to submit their reports in time for the 
next meeting of the NDC. The reports of these two Committees will be 
considered at the time of 11th Five Year Plan. 
(d) Does not arise. 
Meeting of NDC 
†1981. SHRI R.S. GAVAI: Will the PRIME MINISTER be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that a meeting of National Development Council was 
held on 27th and 28th June in Vigyan Bhavan; 
†Original notice of the question was received in Hindi. 
126 

[11 August, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
(b) if so, the issue discussed in the meeting; 
(c) the recommendation made to be implemented in future; and 
(d) the steps Government would take to implement these 
recommendations? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF PLANNING (SHRI 
M.V. RAJASEKHARAN): (a)to (c) The National Development Council met 
under the Chairmanship of the Prime Minister on 27th and 28th June, 2005 to 
consider the Mid-Term Appraisal of the Tenth Five Year Plan and took the 
following decisons: 
1. The NDC expressed broad agreemen t with the goals and policies 
suggested in the Mid-Term Appraisal which could act as a blue print 
for further action on development matters in the Tenth Plan and as the 
starting paint for initiating work on the Eleventh Five Year Plan. The 
Planning Commission was directed to examine a number of valuable 
suggestions made by Chief Ministers during the course of discussions 
which require a review of some of the policies, programmes and 
approaches. 
2. The NDC took note of the concern expressed by the Chief Ministers about 
issues relating to State finances, particularly the effects of the 
recommendations of the 12th Finance Commission, the level of 
permissible market borrowings and interest costs on borrowings as also 
issues relating to mineral royalties and externally aided projects. It was 
decided to set up a Committee separately under the Finance Minister 
to examine relevant issues relating to the debt burden of States and 
debt relief with reference to their debt outstandings against the Natioal 
Small Saving Fund (NSSF). 
3. Recognizing the fact that agriculture and irrigation have been a 
common theme in the interventions of the Chief Ministers, and that 
rejuvenating the agricultural credit system, providing some measure of 
relief to farmers, improving the quality of our extension work, 
attending to the specific needs and problems of dry lands and 
wastelands and enhancing investments in irrigation have emerged as 
common concerns, the NDC agreed  to form a Sub-Committee for 
drawing up implementable action plans in agriculture and related issues. 
The NDC Sub-Committee is expected to submit its report 
127 

RAJYA SABHA [11 August, 2005] 
within the next six months for inclusion in the Approach Paper to the 
Eleventh Five Year Plan. 
4. On the Employment Gurantee Act, the suggestions that payment of 
wages should be mostly in cash since there were problems in movement 
of food grains to backward areas and that being the self-targeting 
programme, the Employment Guarantee should cover non-BPL families 
were noted by the NDC, and it was directed to consider them for inclusion 
in the final draft of the National Employment Guarantee Bill. 
5. To look into the need for providing adequate flexibility in the design of 
Centrally Sponsored Schemes, such as Sarva Shiksha Abhiyan, the 
National Rural Health Mission and Bharat Nirman etc., to take account 
of state level realities and priorities, as well as the feasibility of their transfer 
to States/UTs or amalgamation into four or five broad heads with the 
freedom to develop locally relevant programmes, the NDC directed the 
Planning Commission to consider setting up an Expert Group to develop 
concrete proposals for restructuring the CSS, in consultation with the 
concerned Ministries/Departments. 
6. Recognizing that improvement in physical infrastructure has also 
emerged as a common priority and in creased private participation has 
now become a necessity to mobilize the resources needed to achieve its 
expansion and upgradation, the NDC observed that successful 
promotion of private participation in infrastructure requires a well-designed 
framework of policies in which investors have the assurance that 
standards of services will be maintained and concessions w ill be 
transparently awarded and directed the Central Government to work towards 
evolving such a framework, which could be adopted by the States. 
7. The Planning Commission was directed to begin work on the 
Approach to the Eleventh Five Year Plan with a view to submit it for 
National Development Council's approval by the end of December, 2005. 
(d) Steps have already been initiated on the decisions/directions 
concerning Planning Commission. Besides, Planning Commission has also 
circulated the decisions/directions of the National Development Council 
128 

[11 August, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
to all Central Ministries/Departments as well as State Governments/UTs 
Administrations for taking action as deemed necessary.

1983. SHRI S.S. AHLUWALIA: Will the PRIME MINISTER be pleased to 
state: 
(a) whether pilot projects to provide free food grains to undernourished 
adolescent girls and pregnant and nursing mothers was launched in 
Maharashtra and other States in the recent past; 
131 

RAJYA SABHA [11 August, 2005] 
(b) if so, the details of the project, including names of States/districts 
covered, and likely to be covered; 
(c) whether schemes are being implemented to ensure nutritious food 
intake by children in 0-3 year age group, under Pradhan Mantri Gramodaya 
Yojana (PMGY); and 
(d) the details about the scheme and its implementation in Jharkhand, 
including the number of children covered, amount spent and logistics for its 
implementation, Year-wise since inception of the State, district-wise? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF PLANNING (SHRI 
M.V. RAJASEKHARAN): (a) and (b) Nutritional programme for Adolescent 
Girls (NPAG) was launched, by the Planning Commission in 51 districts 
(including two districts in Maharashtra) for a period of two years i.e. 2002-03 
and 2C03-04 on pilot basis under which food grains were provided to 
adolescent girls and pregnant and Iactating women from BPL families at 
subsidized rates. Undernourished Adolescent Girls (age group 11-19) (weight 
<35 kg) and pregnant and locating women (weight <40 kg) are covered. Free 
food grains @ 6 kg per beneficiary per month, are provided to these 
undernourished persons initially for a period of three months. Those 
beneficiaries who in spite of receiving food grains for th e three consecutive 
months did not show improvement are to be referred to doctor for 
investigation and treatment. They in th e meantime continue to receive food 
grains for the next three months. State-wise list of districts covered under 
NPAG is enclosed as Statement (See be low). The scheme has been revived 
and is to be implemented by Department of Women and Child Development, 
Government of India, from the year 2005-06. 
Under the pilot project, in Maharashtra, the physical and financial progress 
has been nil. The scheme is expected to pick-up in the current year 2005-06. 
(c) and (d) Pradhan Mantri Gramodaya Yojana had six components of 
which Nutrition was one of them. The Nutrition component of Pradhan 
Mantri Gramodaya Yojana (PMGY) was specially designed with the objective 
of encouraging mothers to introduce semi-solid supplements to children in the 
age-group of 6-36 months. States were to provide take-home mixture of 
cereals, pulses and oil seeds to fa milies concerned. PMGY has been 
discontinued from the financial year 2005-06.

1985. DR. GYAN PRAKASH PILANIA: Will the PRIME MINISTER be 
pleased to state: 
(a) the parameters/criteria for granting status of Below Poverty Line to a person; 
(b) whether they are different for urban and rural areas; 
(c) the total number of Below Poverty Line persons in the country with State-
wise break up; 
(d) what percentage it is of total population of the country as well as States; 
(e) whether there is any improvement or deterioration in Below Poverty Line 
scenario in the country; and 
138 

[11 August, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
(f) if so, its details thereof? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF PLANNING 
(SHRI M.V RAJASEKHARAN): (a) and (b) The Planning Commission has 
adopted per capita consumption expenditure needed to attain a minimum amount 
of calorie intake out of food consumption along with a minimum am ount of 
non-food expenditure in order to meet the requirements of clothing, shelter, 
transport etc. as the criterion to determine the persons living below the poverty 
line. The per capita consumption norm has been fixed at Rs. 49.09 per month in 
rural areas and Rs. 56.64 per month in urban areas at 1973-74 prices at national 
level corresponding to a basket of goods and services anchored on a norm of 
per capita daily calorie requirement of 2400 kcal in rural areas and 2100 kcal in 
urban areas. As per the Expert Group on 'Estimation of Proportion and Number 
of Poor' (Lakadawala Committee), the state-specific poverty lines are derived from 
the basket of goods and services consumed by the national poverty line class, 
using state-specific price indices and inter-state price differentials. The prescribed 
per capita consumption expenditure for determination of people living below 
poverty line for different states are regularly updated using state-specific cost of 
living indices, that is, Consumer Price Indices for Agricultural Labourers (CPIAL) 
for rural areas and Consumer Price Indices for Industrial Workers (CPIIW) for 
urban areas. 
(c) and (d) The state-wise total numb er and percentage of persons living 
below the poverty line in the country for both rural and urban areas in 1999-2000 
is given in the Statement (See below). 
(e) and (f) The Planning Commission estimats poverty at national and state 
level from the large sample surveys of Household Consumers Expenditure 
conducted by the National Sample Survey Organization (NSSO) at an interval 
of approximately five years. The latest such survey was conducted in 1999-2000 
(NSS 55m Round). The poverty ratios estimated from the last three large sample

Research in Biotechnology 
1988. SHRIMATI N.P. DURGA: W ill the Minister of SCIENCE AND 
TECHNOLOGY be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that Department of Biotechnology has selected new 
areas for research in the field of Biotechnology; 
142 

[11 August, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
(b) what exactly is bio-separation; 
(c) whether any research is going on in the country on bio-separation; and 
(d) if so, in what way it helps the common man? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF SCIENCE AND 
TECHNOLOGY (SHRI KAPIL SIBAL): (a) Yes, Sir. 
(b) Bio-separation is the process for purification of targeted bio-molecule by 
applying various techniques. Bio-molecules are usually present in very low 
concentrations. Further, the impurities could have physicochemical properties 
similar to those of the target compound of interest. Several separation steps 
are needed to obtain the target molecule  sufficiently pure to make it suitable 
for a specific use. The primary downstream operation is the removal of 
insolubles (e.g. by sedimentation, filtration, centrifugation, permeation by 
membranes), followed by isolation of the compound (e.g. by precipitation, 
extraction, adsorption, separation by membranes) and final purification (e.g. by 
crystallization, chromatography). 
(c) Yes, Sir. 
(d) Bio-separation is useful for various biotechnological applications 
involving large scale purification and protein separation. It is one of the steps 
involved in the process for preparation of therapeutically important compounds, 
antibiotics, food supplements and enzymatic preparations. It also has application in 
water and air purification systems leading to reduction in environmental pollution. 
Gene Silencing 
1989. SHRI NANDI YELLAIAH: Will the Minister of SCIENCE AND 
TECHNOLOGY be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Hyderabad based Centre for Cellular and Molecular Biology (CO 
M.B.) led by Manika Pal Bhadra and Utpal Bhadra under C.C.M.B., Director 
Shri Lalji Singh has unraveled the Mystery behind Gene Silencing paving the way 
for detecting the mechanisms that prevents cancer in human beings; 
(b) if so, the details thereof;

(c) details of action taken so far in the direction of developing these new 
findings towards Pharmaceutical therapy for Patenting and marketing the product 
to save several millions of cancer victims in the world from death, every year; 
(d) whether Government would assure of releasing special package of funds 
in this most important and crucial field of "Gene Silencing" for speedy results; and 
(e) if not, the reasons therefor? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF SCIENCE AND 
TECHNOLOGY (SHRI KAPIL SIBAL): (a) Yes, Sir. 
(b) Dr. Manika Pal Bhadra and Utpal Bhadra first demonstrated that gene 
silencing is involved in heterochroma tin which is required for rapid cell 
division; these results have already been published in the prestigious journal 
Science (2004). In continua tion to their work they recently found that several 
micro RNAs are involved in heterochromatin formation. Diseases coupled with cell 
division and cell proliferation, such as various types of Cancers, appear to be 
controlled by heterochromatin formation and its functioning. Understanding the 
role of gene silencing through micro RNAs thus might pave a way to use it as a 
possible therapy for cancers and other related diseases, which involve cell 
cycle controls. 
(c) and (d) Several measures are being taken in the direction of the 
development of therapy for cancer. Besides preparing a detailed progress report for 
the application of these results for can cer treatment Scientists at CCMB have 
also prepared a detailed document for patent application. The programme as part 
of R&D activity of CCMB is receiving necessary financial support. 
(e) Question does not arise.

THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF SCIENCE AND

145

have been put in place to achieve the above objective to provide infrastructural and

Technology Leadership Initiative (NMITLI) and Drug & Development Promotion

schemes take adequate care to ensure that inventions from scientific institutions and

2019. SHRI S.M. LALJAN BASHA: Will the Minister of SHIPPING, 
ROAD TRANSPORT AND HIGHWAYS be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government or the NHAI have received any proposal for a 
uniform system of giving driving licences from the Road Safety Forum in 
Andhra Pradesh; 
(b) the proposals under consideration for arranging modern and efficient driving 
licence examinations and efficient system of giving licences, nation-wise; 
(c) whether poor and varied systems of giving licences for drivers in the country 
has created a pool of unsafe and dangerous drivers along highway; 
(d) the steps proposed to consider the system of having a national system 
of giving driving licences; and 
(e) the reasons for not taking up this proposal? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF SHIPPING, ROAD 
TRANSPORT AND HIGHWAYS (SHRI K.H. MUNIAPPA): (a) and (b) 
Chapter-ll of the Motor Vehicles Act,  1988 and Chaper-ll of the Central 
Motor Vehicles Rules, 1989 prescribe a body of rules for testing and 
examination prior to grant of driving licences. These rules also prescribe the 
procedure for granting the licences and the validity in terms of various classes of 
vehicles and the time period. Central Motor Vehicles Rules, 1989 also provides 
for issuance of smart-card based driving licences, based on a standardised 
software, developed and made available by Central Government to the States. 
The States have been empowered to prescribe the date from which such smart-card 
based driving licences shall be issued in the States. 
(c) Compliance with the provisions of Motor Vehicles Act, 1988 and 
Central Motor Vehicles Rules, 1989 and the procedure laid down therein rules 
out licensing of unsafe and dangerous drivers. 
(d) and (e) Section 28 of the Motor Vehicles Act, 1988 empowers the State 
Governments for appointment of the licensing authorities and determining 
their jurisdiction, functions etc. There is no proposal to have a national system of 
giving driving licences as the same is the responsibility

SHRI ASHWANI KUMAR (Punjab): Sir, I rise to take part in a debate whose 
genesis we trace back to a colossal national tragedy that struck this country on 31 st 
October, 1984. Sir, a serving Prime Minister, mother 
214 

[11 August, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
of the nation and leader of millions of In dians, fell victim to the assassins' 
bullets. What followed was indeed a national tragedy of the greatest 
magnitude. It would remain for long a wound that struck at the core of our 
national conscience. It is in that context, Sir, that we discuss this Report, the 9th 
in a series of reports that sought to heal the wounds of the nation and bring to 
justice those guilty of the crimes against humanity. It would, therefore, be my 
endeavour not to make this debate into a partisan debate but to draw attention of this 
august House and, through this august House, of the nation, to the facts that we 
must consider and to the challenges that we face in the future. 
Sir, 31st October, 1984 was akin to that moment in history when as 
someone said, centres cease to hold and nations are called upon to find their feet, 
their space, and to reassert their ethos and their conscience. A violent mob in 
Delhi and in some other parts of the country reacted in the manner that it did. 
Totally indefensible! No one in his right mind can directly or indirectly defend the 
gruesome-acts that followed the assassination of late Shrimati Indira Gandhi. 
We then, Sir, sought about devising mechanisms to heal the wounds and to 
apply balm to those who were affected and to ensure that such incidents 
would not recur. And in that series. Sir, the Nanavati Report came up with 
certain recommendations. The substance of the Report on the political side 
decisively and unambiguously exonerates the top leadership of the Congress Party 
which for 21 long years has been victim of an insidious and an orchestrated 
campaign of calumny an d viciousness. That lie stands nailed. The 
Commission did point a finger at a few individuals, and made ten 
recommendations in all. Nine recommendations, Sir, were accepted in toto, as 
indicated in the ATR. There was a difference of opinion with respect to action 
against one individual. That also, Sir, has since been accepted and the 
resignation of the Minister must finally put a lid on that aspect as well. After the 
Prime Minister's statement in the Lok Sabha yesterday. Sir, this nation cannot 
be in doubt as to the resolve of the Government; as to the commitment of the 
Congress Party to effectuate full and complete reparation in the form of 
restitution, compensation, rehabilitation,  and succour to all those who were 
affected. The Prime Minister and the Ho me Minister have in their respective 
statements assured the nation, through their address in the Lok Sabha that all 
possible steps required to be taken to correct the aberrations in the delivery 
system of justice and to ensure full and total responsiveness of administration, 
if such events were to recur should leave none in doubt as to the commitment 
215 

RAJYA SABHA [11 August, 2005] 
and resolve of this Government and of the Congress Party. But, Sir, there is a 
much wider element in this debate. I have heard, as I always do, with great 
attention what Raj Nath Singhji had to say. I was disappointed, Sir. I had 
thought that this debate would not be used to score political points. The tragedy 
was too great, the agony is indescribable in words and it would need a lot of 
wisdom, sagacity, generosity and commitment to ensure that such aberrations 
do not wound the conscience of the nation yet again. But, what do we find, Sir? 
In stark defiance of the conclusions of  the Report, which has nailed the lie 
against the Congress Party, it was again asserted that the Congress was 
responsible for the carnage. Here is a party which asked one of its Ministers to 
go, even though we are convinced that in law there is no case of culpability 
against him, and yet this Party and the Government is being called to account by 
those whose hands are sullied in the blood of thousands of people in Gujarat. Sir, I 
can understand a political party seeking to make a political point. But these are 
issues of political morality; these are issues that confront the ethos of a nation; 
all that the nation stands for and the values of the Republic. I should have 
thought that the level of debate would be raised so that in our collective wisdom 
we can give a direction to the people and take direction from the felt sensitivities 
of the people. 
Sir, I would like to congratulate the Prime Minister and the Government for 
being responsive to the felt perceptions and sensitivities of the people. The Prime 
Minister said in so many words that the sentiments of the people of India 
would be respected. Ultimately, Sir, it is perception that promotes reality to 
meaning and in that vein and in that spirit, we have abided by the sentiments of 
this House and the sentiments of the people of India. We are not obvious of the 
fact that the wounds of 1984 still fester in the hearts of people. I come from 
Punjab, Sir, and I know what 1984 riots meant and what the assassination of 
Shrimati Indira Gandhi meant to the multitude of the people of India. I implore, 
particularly my esteemed friends of the Akali Dal not to discuss this grave and 
critical issue in" an idiom that would incite passions. It has taken a lot of 
blood and many years of turmoil to get our country back on its feet. In 
seeking to score political points, let us not derail the process of reconciliation, 
that is now finding firm ground in the conscience of this nation. Sir, this 
debate is important, it is important because, in my belief, it would cement the 
216 

[11 August, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
foundations of democracy. I am gratified and grateful to you, Mr. Chairman, Sir, for 
having permitted this debate, because through this debate, we ought to focus 
on the injustices and the tragedies that struck our nation only to ensure that such 
tragedies do not recur and in that spirit, Sir, I rise only to make a point that man's 
inclination for injustice makes democracy necessary. And man's capacity for 
justice makes democracy possible. And, therefore, Sir, in exercising our 
democratic rights today in this House of expressing ourselves, the purpose 
should not be to fix liability where none can be fixed and which, in fact, has 
been denied by the successive Commissions, but to tell the nation that the 
entire political spectrum in this country speaks in one voice to ensure that these 
instances would not recur. That, Sir, should be the focus of this debate, and it is 
in that spirit, on behalf of my party that I rise to take part in this debate. 
Sir, justice is the final measure of power. I make bold to state that we need to 
ensure that justice is not only done, but is seen to be done. And in that context 
the Prime Minister has stated that every single suggestion and recommendation 
made by Justice Nanavati towards securing of justice to those who are aggrieved 
shall be taken. 
I would only like to conclude by adding that we, in this country are not 
committed to rough, ready and roughshod justice. We have a Constitution, we have 
an established procedure of law through which culpability and gu ilt is to be 
fixed. In our anxiety to demonstrate our resolve to bring ability to justice, let 
nothing be done that is outside the ambit of law, that does not measure up to the 
Constitutional requirements so that nation should not accuse us compromising 
one value of the Republic in order to subserve the other. We are capable of; it is 
within our genius, Sir, to reconcile the two imperatives to ensure justice 
according to law: That is the burden of my intervention, and that is what I 
recommend to this august House. Thank you very much.

DR. PC. ALEXANDER (Maharashtra): Sir, ever since the Commission's Report 
was tabled in Parliament, we have been reading about expressions of 
disappointment not only from political personalities, but also from eminent jurists. 
Probably the five years' time that it took in bringing out the Report and the fact 
that Shri Nanavati had a high reputation as a founder of the Supreme Court had 
created a lot of expectations among the people about this Report, but the Report, 
when it came, disappointed many people, and disappointed, particularly, the Sikh 
Community which had been waiting for some redressal of the grievances and 
injustices they had suffered in the 1984 events. I should say, with due apologies 
to the Home Minister, that the Action Taken Report aggravated the 
disappointment. Even though the Government took six months to prepare the 
ATR, when it came to the notice of the people, they found that it was more 
disappointing than the Report itself. In fact, if the hon. Prime Minister had not 
taken the trouble of explaining to the Lok Sabha what he is planning to do, and if 
he had not taken the trouble of telling us in the Rajya Sabha today that some of 
the points raised in the Report would be very strongly acted upon, the ATR 
would have created much disappointment and even trouble for the whole country. 
To a very large extent, the Prime Minister's intervention, yesterday and today, has 
neutralised some of the bad effect of the ATR. I only wonder, as an old 
administrator, why those who prepared the original draft, did not take proper care 
usually taken before it is submitted to political levels? I leave it at that. 
This morning, I listened to a statement by a very senior hon. Member of this 
House not even the very appointment of this Commission was not necessary, 
said that it was rushed through, and after the Question Hour, during the period 
known as the Zero Hour, it had been hastly agreed to. I choose to differ from 
him. I think, it has served a good purpose. If the feelings of the Sikh community, 
today, are somewhat assuaged, it is largely because of the fact that this Report has 
indicated certain action points. And, the Prime Minister has said that he will 
follow it up promptly. I will just mention three main issues which have been 
thrown up by this Report.

The first issue is the unequivocal stat ement in the Report that the carnage, 
which took place in the first week of November, 1984, was not just the result of 
a sudden outburst of anger or just the expression of an uncontrolled fury on the 
part of the people who could not reconcile themselves to the murder of a very 
highly respected and beloved Prime Minister. The Report says that could have 
been true in the initial stages, on the 31st of October and, probably, a few hours 
later, but very soon it had been taken over by those who had other designs. And 
this finding of the Commission is certainly a very damaging one. It shows that it 
was an organised effort on the part of some people. I do not have to describe the 
conclusions of the Report on that part of it. And I would earnestly request the 
Prime Minister and the Home Minister to give the utmost importance to these 
observations in the Report, and to show, by very quick action, that they have 
taken a serious note of this and those responsible for these misdeeds would be 
brought to book soon. The second issue raised in this Report, which should have 
deserved much better consideration than it had on the part of those who 
prepared the ATR, is regarding the police administration in our country. The 
statements in the administration report, a very brief report, speaks volumes. In 
fact, it is the greatest indictment that one can think of from a judge, who was 
heading a commission, about the state of affairs in the police today. I will just 
read that one sentence, "If the police ha d taken prompt and effect steps, very 
probably, so many lives would not have been lost and so many properties would 
not have been looted, destroyed or burnt". To say that the inaction on the part of 
the police or negligence on the part of the police, which the Report very clearly 
brings out, has contributed to the loss of life, forget the loss of property, would 
ever linger in our mind till appropriate action is taken against these 
policemen. I can assure the hon. Minister that the mere fact that a person who 
has retired from service is no excuse for not proceeding against that person, if he 
was guilty of criminal conduct, disciplinary action may not be possible but if 
the criminality is proved in a court of law, that would be a compensation for those 
who are aggrieved. I would request the hon. Home Minister to consider, very 
seriously, a total revamp of the police administration in our country. We are still 
managing the police administration on the traditions that had been left behind by 
the British. Even though we have advanced so much in the prospective of our 
democracy, we are still continuing the old traditions, and that is why we find 
indifference, police brutality, police looking the other side when some

ORAL ANSWERS TO QUESTIONS 
Schemes of National Horticulture Board 
*281. SHRI MATILAL SARKAR: Will the Minister of AGRICULTURE 
be pleased to state: 
(a) the percentage of horticultural land in the country, State-wise; 
(b) the number of schemes implemented by the National Horticulture Board 
in the country and in the North-Eastem States; 
(c) the percentage of the horticultural produce processed during the years 
2002-03, 2003-04 and 2004-05; and 
(d) whether Government are planning for processing horticultural 
produce in a larger quantity to avoid wastage of the produce? 
THE MINISTER OF AGRICULTURE (SHRI SHARAD PAWAR): (a) to 
(d) A Statement is laid on the Table of the House. 
Statement 
(a) to (d) The State-wise percentage of area under horticultural crops with 
reference to total area under cultivation in the country is given in the 
Statement-I (See below). The National Horticulture Board is implementing 
five schemes in the country including North-Eastem States. These schemes are (i) 
Development of Commercial Horticulture through Production and Post-
harvest Management, (ii) Capital Investment Subsidy for 
Construction/Modernization/Expansion of Cold Storage and Storages for 
Horticulture Produce, (iii) Technol ogy Development and Transfer for 
Promotion of Horticulture, (iv) Market Information Service for 

RAJYA SABHA [12 August, 2005] 
Horticulture Crops and (v) Horticulture Promotion Services. The total 
quantity of fruit and vegetables processed during 2002-03, 2003-04 and 2004-
05 is 18 lakh tonnes, 20 lakh tonnes and 22 lakh tonnes respectively which is 
around 1:4 per cent of the production. The Ministry of Food Processing 
Industries is implementing Plan Schemes for encouraging development of 
food processing industries. The schemes includes (a) Technology 
Upgradation/Establishment/Modernization of Food Processing for which 
assistance is given in the form of grant, subject to 25% of the plant and 
machinery and technical civil works subject to a maximum of Rs. 50 lakhs in 
general areas and 33.33% upto Rs. 75 lakhs in difficult areas, and (b) Scheme 
for Infrastructure Development for Food Park for which assistance is given in 
the form of grant subject 25% of the project cost in general areas and 33.33% 
in difficult areas subject to a maximum of Rs. 4 crores for provision of 
common facilities like cold storage, food testing and analysis laboratory, 
effluent treatment plant, common processing facilities, power, water supply, 
etc.

SHRI MATILAL SARKAR: Sir, my first supplementary is, the total 
processed horticultural produce is stated to be 1.4 per cent only of the total 
agro-produce. But, Sir, in the Annual Report, the percentage appears to be fairly 
larger than what is stated here. Sir, particularly, in the North-East Region where 
there is heavy rainfall, if water catchment programme is taken extensively, more 
areas can be brought, under horticulture. Sir, my question is, why is the 
percentage comparatively so small in respect of horticulture? And, what steps 
the Government propose to take to expand the areas under horticulture, 
whatever it is possible? Because in Madhya Pradesh, Uttar Pradesh, Punjab, 
the percentage is very low. ...(Interruptions)... 
MR. CHAIRMAN: You have put your question. Let him reply. 
...(Interruptions)... 
SHRI MATILAL SARKAR: This seems to be very low. What is the 
programme of the Government in this regard? 
MR. CHAIRMAN: Mr. Sarkar, you have put the question. Let him reply. 
SHRI SHARAD PAWAR: Mr. Chairman, Sir, the production figure of 1.4 
per cent which the hon. Member has given is not the country's production. 
This figure of 1.4 per cent is in respect of processed production. Out of total 
production, only 1.4 per cent is processed. That is why we are very weak in 
agro-processing area. That is the reas on, we have introduced a number of 
schemes through agro-processing units. 
The second thing which the hon. Member has asked is how to increase the area 
under horticulture. In fact, this is the reason why the new scheme has been 
introduced, i.e., the Horticulture Mission, where a substantial monetary 
provision has been made, and in five year time, we would like to double the 
total area under horticulture in the country. 
SHRI MATILAL SARKAR: Sir, my s econd supplementary is this. The 
setting up of processing units for fruits and vegetables may be encouraged 
among the youth through self-employment schemes. These youth should be 
specially trained for this purpose; and they should be extended financial 
facilities through banks. What is the programme in 
4 

[12 August, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
this regard? Is there any programme wi th the Government to encourage the 
youth for self-employment in the field of food processing? 
SHRI SHARAD PAWAR: Sir, the programme under the Ministry of Food 
Processing is like this. In fact, as I said, the total capacity of the fruit and 
vegetable processing industry on the 1 st of January, 2005 is 19.24 lakh 
tonnes only. What the Government has decided is to encourage this sector. 
That is why a number of decisions have been taken. For instance, recently, in 
order to give boost to the growth of food processing industry, the Government 
has allowed under the Income-Tax Act, a deduction of hundred per cent of 
profit for five years and twenty-five per cent profit for the next five years. 
That is one of the decisions which the Government has taken just to 
encourage various sections. In addition to it, there are some other schemes, 
where some subsidy has been provided to those who are going to set up a 
specific unit which will be useful for ag ro-processing or fruit-processing or 
vegetable-processing. There is no specific scheme for younger generation. 
These schemes are available for everybody.

AND FAMILY WELFARE be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government are aware that almost ten thousand people die in 
Chhattisgarh due to Sickle Cell disease; 
(b) whether Government would consider establishing a Sickle Cell Unit 
in the State to provide test facilities at all district centres in Chhattisgarh; and

RAJYA SABHA [12 August, 2005] 
THE MINISTER OF HEALTH AND FAMILY WELFARE (DR. 
ANBUMANI RAMDOSS): (a) to (c) A Statement is laid on the Table of the House. 
Statement 
According to Indian Council of Medical Research (ICMR), Sickle Cell disease is 
prevalent in various States in different parts of the country including Chhattisgarh. 
Though a number of deaths occur in Chhattisgarh due to this disease, the ICMR and the 
Government of Chhattisgarh have informed that there is no authentic data available in 
this regard. The disease is a genetic disorder due to defective haemoglobin structure and is 
generally prevalent in the tribal areas. This being a hereditary disease, prevention is the 
only remedy available which includes creating awareness in the affected region. 
The Chhattisgarh Government has informed that a decision has already been taken by the 
State Government to establish Sickle Cell Solubility Test Facilities at all the sector, 
block and district level Government hospitals along with Haemoglobin 
Electrophoresis facilities at all the district level Government hospitals for detection of 
Sickle Cell disorders. In addition, ICMR has informed that testing facilities have been 
set up at Raipur Medical College under ICMR WHO programme to screen antenatal 
pregnant women for prevalence of Sickle Cell anaemia.

*283. PROF. P.J. KURIAN: Will the Minister of ENVIRONMENT AND 
FORESTS be pleased to state: 
(a) whether the Government have approved the Pampa Action Plan to clean

THE MINISTER OF ENVIRONMENT AND FORESTS (SHRI A RAJA): 
(a) to (d) A Statement is laid on the Table of the House. 
Statement 
Question No. 283 to be raised by Prof. P.J. Kurian 
(a) and (b) The first phase of the project for abatement of pollution of River 
Pamba at Sabrimala and Pamba in Kerala has been approved for an amount of 
Rs. 18.45 crore under National River Conservation Plan (NRCP) with 
Central share in the project cost of Rs. 12.92 crore and the State Govt.'s share 
of Rs. 5.53 crore. 
(c) and (d) Under the above project, th e first installment amounting to Rs. 
75 lakhs under the Central share has already been released. As the area where 
works are proposed to be taken up falls under the Periyar Tiger Reserve, 
specific clearance from the Apex Cour t is required by the user agency 
(Travancore Devaswom Board) for diversion of forest land for undertaking 
these works, for which necessary recommendation has already been made by 
the Standing Committee of National Board of Wildlife (NBWL). 
As regards the remaining phases of the Pamba Action Plan, the detailed 
project reports are to be submitted by the State Government as per the Master 
Plan, the preparation of which has been entrusted to a professional agency by 
the State Government.

(a) to (d) 71 river stretches are polluted inter-alia due to discharge of domestic and

A Statement is laid on the Table of the House. 
Statement 
(a) No, Sir. In its Mid-Term appraisal of .the Tenth Five Year Plan (2002-
2007), the Planning Commission has projected growth of GDP at 2001-02 
prices in agriculture, including allied sectors of forestry and logging, and 
fishing, at 4.0 per cent and 3.2 per cent during 2005-06 and 2006-07

(b) and (c) As indicated in the Mid-Term Appraisal of the Tenth Plan, the 
growth rate in 2002-03 the first year of the Tenth Plan was negative (-6.8 per 
cent) which reflected the impact of the severe drought that adversely affected 
agricultural production in several States/regions in the country. Favourable 
weather facilitated revival of agricultural growth, which improved to 9.5% in 
2003-04. However, in the subsequent year, i.e. 2004-05 serious deficiency in 
rainfall led to deterioration in performance in the agriculture sector, and as a 
result, growth rate in agriculture decelerated to 1.1 per cent. The inability of 
Indian agriculture to withstand weather related shocks mainly reflects the fact 
that there has been steady decline in public investment in real terms in 
agriculture, including allied sectors, over successive Five Year Plans. This in 
turn reflects decline in investment towards irrigation and water management. 
With a view to increase agricultural production, Government has adopted 
a multi progned strategy for addressing  specific segments of agriculture to 
ensure higher productivity. These initiatives are in the areas

an overall thrust towards diversification into higher value produces and 
plantations. Initiatives taken towards these areas include launch of the National 
Horticulture Mission, undertaking activities with a Mission approach for 
enhancing productivity and quality of cotton, oilseeds, pulses and coarse 
grains. The Union Budget for 2005-06 has underscored the importance of 
providing enhanced credit coverage to the farming community as a 
consequence of which Rs. 1,15,242 Crores was disbursed in 2004-05. Credit

accelerated irrigation technology progra mme, strengthening of agricultural 
marketing infrastructure, development of backward and forward linkages

producing larger and better quality of fruits, flowers and vegetables.

through inland aquaculture. Livestock and Dairying have also received 
greater attention through enhanced budget outlays as well as defined policies 
towards cross-breeding and delineation of disease free zones.

Agenda of meeting of the National Commission on Population 
*287. SHRI S. ANBALAGAN: Will the Minister of HEALTH AND 
FAMILY WELFARE be pleased to state: 
(a) whether the first meeting of the recently constituted National 
Commission on Population was held recently; 
34 

[12 August, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
(b) if so, the agenda of the meeting and its outcome thereof; 
(c) whether any specific decisions were taken to control the explosion of population 
in the country; if so, the details thereof and if not, the reasons therefor; 
(d) whether it is a fact that the Prime Minister announced during the meeting that 
the Population Policy of the country does not encourage incentives and 
disincentives; and 
(e) if so, the manner in which Government propose to control 
population without any incentives and disincentives? 
THE MINISTER OF HEALTH AND FAMILY WELFARE (DR. 
ANBUMANI RAMADOSS): (a) to (c) Yes, Sir. The first meeting of the reconstituted 
National Commission on Population (NCP) was held under the Chairmanship of the 
Hon'ble Prime Minister on 23rd July, 2005. The meeting discussed the following 
items: 
0) Approach to issues of Population Stabilisation based on National 
Common Minimum Programme (NCMP); 
(ii) Learning from Southern States; and 
(iii) Population challenge in demographically weaker States and appropriate 
Strategies. 
In course of detailed discussions on the agenda items, the importance of providing need 
based, client centered, demand driven and high quality services to the beneficiaries, while 
recognizing the need for empowerment of women and their right to make informed 
choices, was emphasized. Such services would enhance the quality of reproductive 
life of the population enabling country to achieve the goal of population stabilization. The 
following two decisions were taken: 
(i) There should be an Annual Health Survey of all districts, which could be 
published annually so that health indicators at district level are periodically 
published, monitored and compared against benchmarks. 
(ii) The Ministry of Health and Family Welfare should set up five groups of 
experts for studyingxthe population profile of the States of Bihar, Uttar 
Pradesh, Rajasthan, Madhya Pradesh and Orissa to identify weaknesses 
in the health delivery 
35 

RAJYA SABHA (12 August, 2005] 
systems and to suggest measures that would be taken to improve the 
health and demographic status of the States. 
(d) and (e) Yes, Sir. The tenet of the Population Policy regarding voluntary and 
informed choice while availing of family welfare services, without any 
incentive/disincentive was emphasized at the meeting. 
Providing incentives and disincentives are not very relevant for population 
stabilization measures. As a matter of fact, on occasions, they can prove to be counter 
productive. The population stabilization requires a holistic approach to the problem. The 
Government has recently launched National Rural Health Mission (NRHM), which seeks to 
provide integrated comprehensive primary healthcare services, especially to the poor and 
vulnerable sections of the society throughout the country with special focus on 18 
States. The objective of the NRHM is to provide accessible and reliable primary 
health care services so as to achieve the Goals of National Population Policy and 
National Health Policy.

and state: 
(a) the reasons for which Government do not wish to display extent of pesticides on 
labels of food items by amending the Food Adulteration (Prevention) Rules, 1955 
keeping in view the concern for health of the common people; 
(b) whether Government are aware that pesticides have been found exceeding the 
prescribed limit in several food products and cold drinks and they affect the public 
health adversely; and 
(c) if so, by when Government would make arrangements for display of the extent of 
pesticides on the labels of food items? 
THE MINISTER OF HEALTH AND FAMILY WELFARE (DR. 
ANBUMANI RAM DOSS): (a) to (c) As per the provisions of the 
†Original notice of the question was received in Hindi. 
36 

[12 August, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
Prevention of Food Adulteration (PFA) Rules, 1955, the names of ingredients used 
in the product shall be declared on the label in descending order of their composition 
by weight or volume as the case may be. Similar provisions have been prescribed by Codex 
Alimeniarious Commission which is an international organization for standardization of 
food products. All the countries in the world follow the practice of declaration of 
the ingredients on the label. 
Pesticides are not used as an ingredient in preparation of any food products. 
Pesticide residues comes in food through use of pesticides upon food crops or during 
storage of food grains. As stated above, there is no practice in any country or any 
provisions under CODEX to display the extent of pesticides on the label of food items. 
There is. therefore, no proposal under consideration for displaying limit of pesticides on 
the label of food items under PFA Rules, 1955. 
In order that the contaminants in food products do not exceed the safe limits, the 
maximum tolerance limits for pesticide residues in food products have been prescribed 
under prevention of Food Adulteration (PFA) Rules, 1955, Any violation of the limits 
prescribed is punishable under law. 
Studies have been conducted by Ministry of Health and Family Welfare during the 
years 1988-89,1993-94 and 2000-01. All these studies reveal that the pesticide residues 
detected in various foods are within the tolerance limits prescribed under the PFA 
Rules, 1955, except in some cases where the residues exceeded the prescribed limits.

The major reasons for high infant and neonatal mortality are poor nutrition of 
mothers and new boms, acute respiratory infections, diarrhoeal diseases and inadequate 
access to maternal and new born care. The causes for low birth weight primarily include

The thrust of agriculture policy continues to be on schemes and

choices.

supposes significant increase in public investment so as to bring about 
increase in area under irrigation. 
Fluctuations in agricultural production adversely affect the financial 
position of farmers. In order to help farmers to tide over the situation, the 
Government announced in June, 2004 several credit-related measures like 
doubling the flow of credit in three years, enhancing the coverage of 
institutional credit through Kisan Credit Cards, restructuring of loans etc.

(c) and (d) The growth rate of agriculture including allied sectors of forestry and 
logging, and fishing during each year of Tenth Five Year Plan in real terms (at 
1993-94 prices) was (-7) per cent during 2002-03, the first year of Tenth Plan, 9.6

growth in agricultural GDP for the first three years of the Tenth Plan therefore works 
out to a modest rate of 1.2 per cent compared with the targeted annual average 
growth of 4 per cent. 
- (e) The year 2002-03, the first year of the Tenth Plan, witnessed a sharp decline 
in agricultural growth by (-) 7.0 per cent due to the severe drought that affected several 
States/regions in the country. The year 2003-04, the second year of the Tenth Plan, 
witnessed a very favourable rainfall, which pushed up agricultural growth to 9.6 per 
cent. This also reflected the very low base of agricultural GDP in 2002-03. The 
year 2004-05, the third year of the Tenth Plan, witnessed deficient rainfall from the 
Southwest monsoon, which adversely affected kharif crop production in many 
States. Though the deficiency in rainfall (-13%) in 2004 was far less serious than 
that in 2002 (-19%), it pulled down growth in agriculture to a modest rate of 1.1 
per cent. 
(f) The inability of agriculture sector to withstand weather related shocks mainly 
reflects the decline in public investment over successive Five Year Plans. This in turn 
reflects serious deficiency in irrigation facilities for agriculture. Union Budget for 2005-
06 has, therefore, provided higher outlays for irrigation. The outlay on Accelerated 
Irrigation Benefits Programme (AIBP) has been raised to Rs. 4,800 crore from Rs. 
2,800 crore in 2004-05. Similarly, a sum of Rs. 400 crore has been allocated for 
promoting micro-irrigation through drip and sprinkler irrigation in 2005-06. Other thrust 
areas include horticulture, agricultural credit and development of livestock and fisheries. 
The National Horticulture Mission, which was launched in May, 2005, aims at doubling 
production of horticulture crops by 2011-12. As regards agricultural credit, the 
disbursement in 2004-05 amounted to Rs. 1,15,242 crore, which represented an 
increase of 34% over the previous year. It is proposed to increase the credit flow to

years.

become ineligible for fresh credit as their earlier debts have been 
categorized as sub-standard or doubtfull shall be rescheduled as 
per the guidelines so that such farmers become eligible for fresh 
credit.

fresh loans.

farmers who have been declared as defaulters and have become 
ineligible for fresh credit. Banks have also been advised to review cases 
where credit has been denied on th e sole ground that a loan account 
was settled through compromise or write offs.

other drugs. There is no specific norms or guidelines to determine as to which 
drugs can be classified as life saving drugs. Every drug , in general, is 
considered useful in saving and prolonging of life. 
The 74 bulk drugs specified in the First Schedle of the Drugs (Prices 
Control) Order, 1995 (DPCO, 95) and the formulations based thereon are 
under price control and their prices are fixed/revised by the National 
Pharmaceutical Pricing Authority (NPPA)  in accordance with the provisions

Statement 
Steps taken by Government for protection and conservation of tigers 
and other wildlife 
Steps taken by the Government for protection and conservation of tigers 
and other wildlife are as under: 
(i) Legal protection has been provided to wild animals against hunting and 
commercial exploitation under the provisions of the Wildlife 
(Protection) Act, 1972. 
(ii) Several rare and endangered sp ecies of wild animals have been 
included in the Schedules of Wildlife (Protection) Act, 1972, 
thereby giving it highest degree of protection. 
(iii) The Wildlife (Protection) Act, 1972 has been amended and made more 
stringent. The punishment in cases of offences has been enhanced. 
The Act also provides for forfeiture of any equipment, vehicle or 
weapon that has been used for committing any wildlife offence. 
122 

[12 August, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
(iv) Central Bureau of Investigation (CBI) has been empowered under the 
Wildlife (Protection) Act, 1972 to apprehended and prosecute wildlife 
offenders. 
(v) Government of India has set up Regional and Sub-regional Offices for 
wildlife preservation in major export and trade centres of the country 
to prevent smuggling of wild animals and their products. 
(vi) Financial and technical help is provided to the States under various 
Centrally Sponsored Schemes, viz. Project Tiger, Project Elephant and 
Development of National Parks and Sanctuaries for enhancing the capacity 
and infrastructure of the States for providing effective protection to wild 
animals. 
(vii) A National Wildlife Action Plan, 2002—16 was adopted by the 
Indian Board for Wildlife under the Chairmanship of Prime Minister in 
January, 2002. The plan outlines the strategy for conservation and 
protection of wildlife in the country. 
(viii) Government of India is a signatory to many international 
conventions concerning biodiversity conservation and control of 
illegal trade in wild flora and fauna. 
(ix) Bilateral agreements have been signed with Nepal and Republic of 
China for controlling trans-boundary illegal trade in wildlife. 
(x) A Global Tiger Forum of tiger ra nge countries has been created for 
addressing international issues related to tiger conservation. 
(xi) A proposal for creating a Wildlife Crime Control Bureau has been made.

Statement-IV 
Steps taken for Protection of Tigers and other wildlife The following 
measures have been taken at the Govemment of India level to protect tiger and 
other wild animals: 
(i) Legal protection has been provided to wild animals including tigers 
against hunting and commercial exploitation under the provisions 
of the Wildlife (Protection) Act, 1972. (ii) Financial and technical help 
is being extended to the States under 
Centrally Sponsored Schemes for enhancing the capacity and 
infrastructure to provide effective protection to wild animals, (iii) The 
Central Bureau of Investigation (CBI) has been empowered 
under the Wildlife (Protection) Act, 1972 to apprehend and 
prosecute wildlife offenders, (iv) The Ministry of Home Affairs has 
addressed all State Governments 
to lend a helping hand to the field formations to curb poaching 
and illegal trade in wildlife. 
137 

RAJYA SABHA [12 August, 2005] 
(v) A National Wildlife Action Plan (2002-2016) has been launched with 
several action points and priority projects for conservation and protection of 
wildlife in the country. 
(vi) Independent monitoring of tiger reserves has been done by a panel of 
experts drawn as per the normative guidelines of the Ministry. A 
standardized format for evaluation has been prescribed for monitoring and 
evaluation, based on the framework of the World Commission of Protected 
Areas (IUCN). 
(vii) A tiger habitat and population evaluation system' has been developed in the 
GIS domain, with inputs from the scientists of Wll, involving the state 
officials and field staff. Based on this, the Project Tiger Directorate of the 
Ministry has refined the procedure with a peer review mechanism comprising of 
independent experts, both national and international (IUCN) for overseeing the 
primary data collection. 
(viii) Tiger presence and its breeding status have been mapped for the entire 
country at taluk level amplification in the GIS domain for an assessment 
of habitat fragmentation.

Problem of leprosy in India 
2127. SHRI RAVI SHANKAR PRASAD: Will the Minster of HEALTH 
AND FAMILY WELFARE be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that India has the highest burden of leprosy in the world; 
(b) if so, what is the extent of this menace indicating the sensitive regions in the 
country; and 
(c) what is the action plan of Government to control this desease? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HEALTH AND 
FAMILY WELFARE (SHRIMATI PANABAKA LAKSHMI): (a) Yes, Sir. 
(b) The total number of recorded cases in India at the end of March, 2005 were 
1,48,910 and the Prevalence Rate of Leprosy at the end of March, 2005 was 1.34 
per 10,000 population. In 11 States/UTs Prevalence Rate of leprosy is between 1-
4/10,000 population. These States/UTs are Chhattisgarh, Jharkhand, Chandigarh, D 
& N Haveli and Delhi, Bihar, Goa, Maharashtra, Orissa, U.R and West Bengal. In 
rest of the 24 States/UTs the level of elimination i.e. Prevalence Rate of less than 1 
per 10,000 population has been achieved. 
(c) The Government of India is implementing the National Leprosy Eradication 
Programme for the elimination of leprosy from the country. The details of the 
scheme are:— 
(i) Decentralization and Institutional Development under which State 
Leprosy Societies have been formed in 27 major States and District 
Leprosy Societies in all the Districts in the country which are responsible 
for proper planning, implementation, monitoring and timely 
corrective action. 
160 

[12 August, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
(ii) Integration of Leprosy Services  with General Health Care System 
in the country for better out-reach and utilization of services by 
community. 
(Hi) Early Leprosy Case Detection and Free Multi Drug Therapy to all 
patients through all Government Primary Health Centres, 
Dispensaries and Hospitals in the country. 
Civ) Intensified Public Awareness Campaigns through Mass Media as 
well as local media at periphery. 
(v) Training of General Health Care Staff in leprosy and in disability 
prevention and Care. 
(vi) Prevention of Deformities and Care. 
Government has set a target of achieving leprosy elimination level i.e. 
Prevalence Rate of less than 1 case per 10,000 population at the national 
level by the end of 2005.

Inquiry reports by Commission of Railway Safety 
2166. SHRI VEDPRAKASH P. GOYAL: Will the Minister of RAILWAYS 
be pleased to state: 
(a) the procedure of discharging inquiry reports submitted by the Commission of 
Railway Safety; 
(b) how many inquiry reports have been submitted by the Commission during the last 
one year about railway accidents;

and

THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF RAILWAYS (SHRI R. VELU): 
(a) Commissioners of Railway Safety submit two reports of each enquiry into railway 
accidents. Preliminary Report indicates provisional findings and immediate 
recommendations. Final Report, containing cause of the accident, responsibility 
therefor and recommendations is submitted to Chief Commissioner of Railway Safety 
and copies thereof are forwarded to Railway Board and railway administration of 
zonal Railways and other Commissioners of Railway Safety. Railway administration of 
the concerned Railway initiates action on the report and submits his comments to the 
Chief Commissioner of Railway Safety. Chief Commissioner of Railway Safety submits 
remarks on the Final Report to the Ministry of Railways after scrutinizing the 
comments of concerned railway administration. Ministry of Railways takes a final view 
on the report and comments of the Chief Commissioner of Railway Safety thereon and 
directs zonal railways administrations to implement accepted recommendations. 
(b) and (c) During the last one year from 1.4.04 to 31.3.05, total 19 inquiry reports 
have been submitted by the Commission. As per these inquiry reports, 10 accidents 
were caused due to failure of Railway

accidents were due to equipment failure and incidental.

measures to improve safety Is a continuous process. Measures being taken by 
Indian Railways to minimize incide nce of accidents include adoption of 
suitable modern technology for interlocking and signaling system, 
upgradation of standards of track and rolling stock, modernization of 
maintenance practices, replacement of  over aged assets, upgradation of 
training]aids like simulators, checks on observance of safety precautions and

against those Railway official who are held responsible for the accident

Demand to Recognise Services of Those who Rescue Persons 
in Distress 
SHRI S.S. AHLUWALIA (Jharkhand): Sir, human history is full of instances where 
driven by passion and sympathy, man has rescued his fellow men from distress and peril 
and, I think, any such kind acts of man anywhere on this earth should be 
highlighted not only to acknowledge such good acts but also to provoke others to 
imbibe it. 
Sir, on 10th July, 2005, a marriage party comprising ninety Christian priests travelling 
in a truck met with an accident on its way from Jamankeri village to Goudpil in 
Sambalpur district in Orissa, in which 10 persons died instantly and the remaining 80 
survivors, who were still struggling for life, trapped in the ill-fated truck in a dense forest, 
were rescued by some dedicated social workers who responded to the emergency 
after hearing their cry for help. 
Importantly, credit for this noble humanitarian act that saved eighty precious lives 
goes to a group of volunteers of the local Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh, i.e. R.S.S., 
who rushed to the accident spot and rescued the survivors from the trap without 
considering their caste, creed or religion. 
Sir, this incident brings forth the memory of the incident of crash of a plane carrying 
Haj pilgrims near Charkhi Dadri village, some years back. Soon after take-off from Delhi 
Airport, the plane had crashed. The first rescuers of the survivors were the volunteers of 
the local R.S.S. who were holding their 'shakhas' there. 
I urge upon the Government to appreciate and highlight such noble acts whenever 
and wherever committed by mankind. Thank you, Sir.

Demand for granting exemption from excise duty on industrial units being set up 
in tsunami-affected districts of Tamil Nadu 
SHRIMATI S.G INDIRA (Tamil Nadu): The State Government of Tamil Nadu had done 
everything possible to rehabilitate the tsunami-affected people in the State of Tamil Nadu. 
Tamil Nadu was the most affected State in the recent tsunami. Many measures had 
been taken by the Government of Tamil Nadu to accelerate reconstruction in the tsunami-
hit Tiruvallur, Kancheepuram, Cuddalore, Nagapattinam, Tuticorin and Kanyakumari 
districts. However, it is the process of reconstruction of infrastructure and revitalisation of 
the economy of these districts which alone can ultimately bring real normalcy back to 
these areas. Many international organisations were providing assistance in this 
process. However, there is a need to give a big push to revitalising this economy of the 
tsunami-affected districts as demanded by the hon. Chief Minister of Tamil Nadu. The 
Government of Tamil Nadu had sought to issue a notification granting exemption from 
excise levies for ten years from the date of commercial production on all excisable goods 
manufactured by the industrial units established in the tsunami-affected districts within 
three years from the date of notification. Such exemption had been granted in the past in 
Kutch, Gujarat, Himachal Pradesh and Uttaranchal. The exemption would attract large-
scale investment from corporate industrial houses to restore and improve 
infrastructure and establish industrial units in the tsunami-hit districts. 
Therefore, I urge upon the Government to grant ten years' exemption from excise levies 
as demanded by the hon. Chief Minister for the units to be established in the tsunami-
affected districts in Tamil Nadu.

Demand for continuation of the CGHS for the Retired and serving government 
employees in the country 
SHRI A. VIJAYARAGHAVAN (Kerala): Sir, the Central Government Health Scheme 
(CGHS) is on the verge of closure. More than 45-lakh servicing employees, 5-lakh 
pensioners, former Governors, freedom fighters, Ministers, Judges and Members of 
Parliament are the beneficiaries of the CGHS. It is serving in 24 cities. Sir, the CGHS 
is having 246 dispensaries, 19 polyclinics, 18 laboratories and 86 ISM units in the 
country. The annual Budget of the CGHS is Rs.600 crores. 
It is reported in the newspapers that the CGHS would be replaced with "Health Card" 
through insurance companies. Whereas, the insurance sector has already been privatised. 
The Government has allowed 84 per cent FDI in insurance sector. Hence, the "Health 
Card" would be a hounding ground for corporate and multinational insurance companies.

Demand for conducting common entrance test for defence services in 
vernacular languages 
SHRI RAVULA CHANDRA SEKAR REDDY (Andhra Pradesh): Mr. Vice-
Chairman, Sir, the three wings of Defence Services of our country are 
recruiting youngsters in their organisation. They are conducting a Common 
Entrance Test by holding written test apart from taking physical test for the 
youngsters. The written test is conducted in Hindi and English only. The present 
recruitment system is disadvantageous  to the candidates hailing from non-
Hindi speaking belt, especially, the poor candidates coming from the weaker 
sections. 
The Union Public Service Commission has permitted the use of vernacular 
languages for writing examinations of UPSC. Hence it is requested that the 
youngsters may be permitted to write the Common Entrance Test of the three 
wings of Defence Services in the vernacular language. This will place the 
youngsters of non-Hindi speaking belt on the same level playing field and will, 
definitely, help the youngsters belonging to Southern India in getting 
appointments in Defence Services.

SHRIMATI SYEDAANWARA TAIMUR (Assam): Mr. Vice-Chairman, Sir, 
pollution has become a major problem in our country. Serious pollutants 
including chemical plants, oil refineries, nuclear waste dumps, regular garbage 
dumps, incinerators, PVC, car factories, plastic factories etc. are creating huge 
amounts of pollution. The nitrogen oxides produced by the industry are often 
referred to as pollution, although the substances themselves are not harmful. In 
fact, it is the solar energy (sunlight) that converts these compounds into smog. 
Recycling of garbage and other waste has become necessary because 
landfills are closed and it is causing increasing damage to the environment.

Organisation conducted survey of about 51,000 farm households throughout the country to 
find out whether they would like to continue in agriculture or migrate to the urban areas 
for employment. 
There is an alarming situation prevailing in the rural area that about 40 per 
cent of the farmers wanted to quit agriculture and migrate to urban areas for living. The 
survey was conducted at the behest of the Agriculture Ministry from January to December, 
2003, for the agriculture year 2002-2003, covering farm household spread over 6,638 
villages. Nearly 60 per cent of the households liked farming as a profession,

that only 16 per cent farmers are aware of bio-fertilisers. Irrigated area is 42 per cent 
during Kharif season and 56 per cent during Rabi season. Tube wells are used as a major

The farmers would like to quit farming because the younger generation did

expedite creation of rural infrastructure by giving priority so that large-scale migration of 
the people from farming community to the urban areas could be contained.

THE IMMIGRATION (CARRIERS' LIABILITY) 
AMENDMENT BILL, 2005 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HOME AFFAIRS (SHRI 
S. REGUPATHY): Sir, I move: 
That the Bill to amend the Immigration (Carriers' Liability) Act, 2000, be 
taken into consideration. 
Sir, the Act places on carriers' the lia bility in respect of foreigners brought 
by them in contravention of the Passport  (Entry into India) Act, 1920 and the 
Rules made thereunder. The necessary of the new legislation was felt 
because a large number of passengers at the major international airports were 
found to be coming without valid travel documents, creating problems for 
immigration authorities. It was observed that carriers, airlines, etc. did not 
exercise proper checks of travel documents before allowing passengers to board 
planes in places outside India. It was, therefore, considered necessary to place 
statutory responsibility on carriers, airl ines, etc. bringing passengers not in 
possession of valid travel documents by imposing financial liability on them to 
the tune of one lakh of rupees per passenger brought by them without any valid 
travel documents, for which five exemptions have been given in respect of those 
who come without any valid travel documents. 
One is where the passenger had arrived on a flight or a ship which, 
following departure, had been diverted to India for reasons beyond the control 
of the carriers. An6ther is where a fo reigner has been exempted from the 
requirement of passport or visa by the Central Government. The third one is 
where the passengers are stowaways and the carrier is ready to take its 
passengers back. The fourth one is where a group of foreign tourists, 
consisting of four or more persons sponsored by recognised Indian travel 
agencies, arrive without visa, being authorised on collective visa, that is, permit 
issued to the whole group. The fifth one is where foreigners hold diplomatic or 
official passport and are exempt from the requirements of the visa. For these 
reasons, this amendment has been brought forward.
