SHRI JANARDHANA POOJARY (Karnataka): Mr. Vice-Chairman, Sir, I am standing 
today before the House after seeing the TV programme the other day. At the 
conclusion of the debate there, when the anchor put the question, then one boy 
stated, These Parliament Members are begging, give them." That was the statement 
made by one boy in the debate. Sir, after seeing that, I was subjected to mental 
agony. It was painful and it was intimidating also. So far as the salary was concerned, 
there never used to be any debate in the House. Sometimes, our friends from the Left 
Party used to make a statement that they opposed; we never used to discuss. Sir, 
before starting, I am just bringing to your notice what the Members of Parliament of 
Australia are getting. They are getting $90,000 per annum. If we calculate it at the 
rate of Rs. 45 per dollar, it will come to Rs. 40,50,000/- per annum — more than 
Rs. 3 lakh. So far as the United Kingdom is concerned, they are getting $85,983. In 
Canada, they are getting $68,200 per annum. If we take into consideration Rs. 45 
per dollar, it will run into lakhs. And, what are we getting here? We are getting only 
Rs. 12,000/-. I thank Mr. Suri, I do not know whether he is a self-made man. He 
has taken into consideration the plight of the spouse after the retirement or after the 
death. I don't know whether he has faced any difficulty in his younger age. But what is 
happening in other countries? If you take into consideration these figures, what are 
we getting? Only Rs. 12,000/-! When I entered after the sixth term, I got Rs. 
12,000/- salary after putting in 27 years of service in the Parliament. Is any officer 
getting this much? Even a chaprasi will be getting more than that, But we are not 
begging. We never ask anything for sevice to the. people. When I started my 
practice in 1960, I was getting this amount per day. I am not from a rich family. 
When I used to go to school, I had only trousers, no shirt even. There were no two 
meals. When I completed my law, there was no money for me. I used to take water 
from the public pipe. And you may not believe, Sir, I did not have the money, I came 
from a very poor family, I used to live on one plantain per day. I had nothing. I became 
a lawyer. I had a roaring practice. I had a car. I had everything. I remained the Minister 
of State in the Ministry of Finance for six years and one month. That is a record. I did 
not take a glass of water from any person. I did not make even a single pie. And, Mr. 
V.P Singh is on record stating, "I come from a rich family, but Poojary comes from a 
poor family". But I remained honest. It is not a big thing. Poojary

Action against Al officials 
*302. SHRI B.K. HARIPRASAD: Will the Minister of CIVIL 
AVIATION be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government are aware that  two Air India traffic officers 
were intercepted at the Heathrow Airport at London in early June, 2005 with 
contraband items from India and deport ed back to Mumbai on account of 
their failure to pay up the fine/penalty imposed by the UK Customs; 
(b) whether AI has taken appropriate disciplinary action against the 
errant officials; and 
(c) whether Government will ensure that the crew of our flag carriers 
flying to overseas destinations are constantly drilled to keep away from such 
unlawful activities?

Table of the House. 
Statement 
(a) Yes, Sir. 
(b) Disciplinary action as per the provisions of the Certified Standing 
Orders is being initiated by Air India Management against the two 
employees. 
 
1

RAJYA SABHA [16 August, 2005]

drawing the attention of the employees, particularly the crew, that they should 
strictly follow the customs regulations and any violation of these rules would 
attract severe punishment. Moreover, the following regulations/orders are in 
force to deal with the errant officials:

executives, has clauses under misconduct, which relates to breach of 
Customs Act, FERA, Narcotics Act etc. as well as smuggling, aiding

of staff has clauses under misconduct, which relate to conviction is

(a) Yes, Sir. Government have received complaints regarding non-

point of sale and in the event of a claim, and setting up of in-house grievance 
redressal mechanism in the insurance companies. In pursuance of these 
regulations, the companies have set up in-house grievance redressal 
mechanisms, which are refined from time to time on the basis of feedback 
received by them. In addition to this, fo r grievances relating to settlement of 
claims, policyholders also approach the Government, Insurance Ombudsmen, 
IRDA Grievance Cell, Consumer Fora and the courts. Government on receipt 
of such grievances sends them to insurance companies/Ombudsmen for 
redressal.

SHRI P. CHIDAMBARAM: Sir, the total complaints received by or 
against non-life companies by the ombudsmen is a small proportion of the 
total claims which are received and which are settled, I think, one has to look 
at it in perspective. For example, in 2C04-05, in respect of medi-claim 
policies, that is, medical insurance policies, the number of claims received by 
the four public sector companies by people who had paid for medical 
treatment and, therefore, claiming insurance benefit, was 6,62,815 received in 
that year. The number of claims settled — current claims as well as claims 
made in the earlier years-was 6,73,661. Therefore, the bulk of the claims are 
usually settled. A complaint arises, Sir, when a claim is not settled; when the 
insurance company's answer is disput ed by the insurer. That is when it 
becomes a complaint. The complaints are, as I said, a small number. For 
example, in 2003-04, the ombudsmen r eceived, in all non- life claims against 
the four public sector insurance companies only 5707 complaints; out of 
which, 3528 have been disposed of. Disposal ratio is about 61 per cent. There 
are three levels of complaints redressal—one at the company level, one at the 
ombudsmen level and the last, at the IRDA level. Hon Member is right that 
Government also received some comp laints. But the Government cannot 
become another level of complaints redressal. So, what we do is that, we 
forward the complaint, either to the IRDA's Complaint Redressal Cell or to 
the Ombudsman. They take over the complaints and redress these complaints. 
I think, the complaints are small in number, and they are being handled. But, 
I think, we need to have proper documentation of the complaints. I have 
given instructions about how each complaints should have a unique 
identification number. We hope to put that in place in the next few weeks. 
But I think, the existing complaint redressal machinery is working reasonably 
satisfactorily. If any suggestions are ma de to improve the machinery, I shall 
be very happy to look into those suggestions.

Statement 
(a) to (c) The SEBI (Delisting of Securities) Guidelines, came into 
effect on February 17, 2003. These guidelines govern "voluntary and

solution that is also consistent with the interests of small investors. 
SEBI has not undertaken any review of listing norms for small sized 
issues. 
SHRI MOTILAL VORA: Sir, I had asked whether in order to give 
relief to the small size companies, the securities and Exchange Board of India 
has reviewed the listing and delisting norms, the hon. Minister has replied

Reduction in prices due to VAT 
2226. SHRI N.K. PREMACHANDRAN: Will the Minister of 
FINANCE be pleased to state: 
(a) the number of State Governments that are keeping away from VAT 
regime; 
(b) whether the VAT system resulted in price reduction and whether it 
is a fact that interest of consumers are not being protected and prices have not 
been brought down for most of the commodities, especailly drugs; 
(c) whether any State Government has urged for a Central legislation 
under which the States could take action against those who reap unfair profit; 
and 
(d) whether Government propose to introduce such legislation, if any? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF FINANCE 
(SHRI S.S. PALANIMANICKAM): (a) 10 States/UTs have not yet 
implemented VAT. These are Uttar Pradesh, Uttaranchal, Rajasthan, Madhya 
Pradesh, Chhattisgarh, Jharkhand, Gujarat, Tamil Nadu, Chandigarh and 
Pondicherry. 
(b) The prices of commodities depend on a number of factors and it 
may not be feasible to segregate the impact of VAT on prices. The overall 
rate of inflation, reflected through the Point-to-Point Movement in the 
Wholesale Price Index, itself has declined from 5.70% for the week ending 02 
April 2005 to 4.07% for the week ending 23 July 2005. The prices of drugs 
and medicines have come down in most of the State due to reduction in the 
tax rate from 8% under Sales Tax regime to 4% under VAT. The States are 
closely monitoring the price situation, to ensure that the benefits of VAT are 
passed on to the consumers. The Em powered Committee of State Finance 
Ministers has advised the States  to set up special VAT Cells, inter alia, to 
monitor this aspect. 
(c) and (d) So far, no su ch proposal has been received from any State 
in the context of VAT and the Central Government has no proposal to 
introduce a Central legislation in this regard.

VAT system; and

THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF FINANCE 
(SHRI S.S. PALANIMANICKAM): (a) and (b) VAT is a State subejct under

including rates of tax on various items, has been finalized by the States 
collectively, through the deliberations  in the Empowered Committee of State

kept outside VAT, have already been brought under the purview of VAT.

the categories of 1% or 4% rate of tax, is taxable at the rate of 12.5% which is 
the general or residual rate of tax under VAT.

meetings of the Committee have so far been held on the 11th April, 2005 and 
29th June, 2005. The inaugural meeting of the Council has been held on 5th-
6th August, 2005 at Kochi. The progress in devolution of functions was 
reviewed and it was noted that while in some States, the preliminary work has 
been completed in terms of the assignment of functions to the three levels of 
panchayats, in several more, the matter is pending at the finalization stage. A 
copy of Joint Statement of conclusions arrived at the meeting is at Statement-!

The Minister has now initiated a process of visiting each of the 
States/UTs to review with the authorities concerned the progress in 
implementing the points for action contained in the compendium. It is 
expected that this will accelerate the base  of implementation of provisions of 
Part IX, read with Article 243ZD of the constitutions and bring about greater 
conformity, in both letter and spirit, to the Constitutional provisions of 
Panchayati Raj in all States/UTs concerned. 
He has so far visited Karnataka, West Bengal and Uttaranchal. The 
documents issued at the conclusion of each of these visits are given at 
Statements II, III and IV respectively. 
Statement I 
Joint statement of conclusions arrived at the meeting held at Kochi on 5th 
and 6th August, 2005 
In order to operationalise the provisions of Article 243 G of the 
Constitution, which provides for devolution to empower Panchayati Raj 
Institutions (PRIs) to function as institutions of self-Government for making 
plans and implementing programmes for economic development and social 
justice the first Round Table of State Ministers of Panchayati Raj held at 
Kolkata in July 2004 resolved as follows, under  the heading, "Effective 
Devolution of Functions." 
"the essential step is the identification of activities related to the 
devolved functions with a veiw to attributing each of these activities to 
the appropriate tier of the 3-tier system;" (Item III), 
"On the basis of the identification of activities relating to devolved 
functions, and through the application of the principle of the 
subsidiarity, States/UTs may review/undejtake time bound activity 
120 

[16 August, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
mapping with a view to completing this exercise within the fiscal year 
2004-05;" (Item V), 
"With a view to promoting a measure of irrevocability of devolved 
functions, devolution may be routed through legislative measures or, 
alternatively, by providing a strong legislative framework for 
devolution through executive orders." (Item VIII) 
The First Meeting of the Council of State Ministers of Panchayati Raj 
reviewed the progress in this direction and noted that while in some States, 
the preliminary work has been completed in terms of the assignment of 
functions to the three levels of panchayats, in several more, the matter is 
pending at the finalization stage. 
However in most States, there is a need to take several more 
substantive steps in the direction of reforms for strengthening Panchayats in 
the true letter and spirit of the Constitution. To this end, State Ministers of 
Panchayati Raj reiterated their commitment to address itself the resolutions 
of the Kolkata Round Table with all de liberate speed and resolved to accord 
priority to the specific following steps: 
(i) Internal discussions with State departments will be expedited so as 
to finalise the consensus on Activity Mapping within the State. 
The Union Ministry of Panchayati Raj will be informed of the 
time line for completing this work. 
(ii) With respect to those areas wh ere there is a general consensus as 
to the devolution of functions and activities to all levels of 
Panchayats, States will expedite the issuing of necessary orders to 
operationalise the same. Copies of Government orders/Gazette 
Notifications will be intimated to Ministry of Panchayati Raj. 
(iii) It is desirable for States to fix milestones in Activity Mapping, and 
take preparatory steps through dissemination of draft frameworks 
prepared to the Panchayats, so that they are in a" state of 
preparedness to assume their new responsibilities. The Union

Joint Statement of conclusions arrive d at after the visit of the Union 
Minister for Panchayati Raj and Petrol eum and Natural Gas to Karnataka on 
the 29th April and 1st May, 2005: 
Karnataka has championed the noble cause of empowering Panchayats 
and devolving powers to them since decades. The State has been at the 
forefront of the empowerment of all thr ee levels of Panchayats so that they 
function as institutions of local self-Government in the letter and spirit of 
Part-IX of the Constitution. The recent measures of the Karnataka 
Government stand testimony to its sustained support to Panchayati Raj 
reform. The amendments made to the Karnataka 
123 

RAJYA SABHA [16 August, 2005]

strengthen the Grama Sabha; create an d empower Ward Sabhas; complete 
Activity Mapping; and rationalize and simplify schemes entrusted to the 
Panchayats are examples to be emulated countrywide. The monitoring of the 
actualization of devolution by the Legislative Committees is a significant step 
in the strengthening of Panchayats in the State. The entrustment of schemes 
by the State Government to Panchayats in the current year's budget is a giant 
step forward in matching the functional transfer with funds. Through this 
process, the Panchayats now handle in  excess of Rs. 3500 crores of Plan

implementation of 77 of the 106 recommendations of the Round Tables that 
pertain to it. The Government of Karnataka will address itself with all 
deliberate speed to the remaining recommendations.

devolved upon Panchayats to the respective levels, in the State 
Budget of 2005-06. In the letter and spirit of Article 243 G of the 
Constitution, the Government of Karnataka commit itself to 
following up the devolution of functions and funds with the

have been devolved upon them it is necessary that funds

Audit 
(i) Since local bodies are now institutions of local self-government, it 
is necessary to upgrade the work  of the Director of Local Fund 
Audit (DLFA) and other similar bodies to the level required by 
Constitutional imperatives and, to this end, for DLFA and other 
similar bodies to work in concert with the Comptroller and 
Auditor General of India (C&AG). 
(ii) In recognition of PRIs being institutions of local self-government, 
PRIs themselves should be associ ated with the preparation of 
standards and norms and the emphasis should be on fund 
management and fund tracking, rather than simply on fund flow, 
to ensure greater accountability. 
(iii) In order to ensure that such audit contributes effectively to 
capping, reducing and eventually  eliminating the scope for 
corruption in Panchayati Raj Institutions (PRIs), it is necessary 
that audit and accounting standards appropriate to the work of the 
Panchayats be established and observed. These standards should 
be elementary, simple and easily comprehensible to the elected 
representatives, and should focus on: 
- when transactions should be looked into; 
- what should be monitored; 
138 

[16 August, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
- how the transactions should be documented; and 
- how they should be disclosed. 
(iv) There is need to establish an in ternal audit system at every tier of 
the Panchayati Raj system and to regard C&AG audit (or audit by 
bodies certified or technically guided by C&AG) as 
complementary external audit. 
(v) Audit, to be effective, might include the establishment of a 
National Accounting Standard  Eoard (NASB) for local 
government accounts and be complemented by the establishment 
of audit commissions or similar such regulatory bodies at the 
State level. 
(vi) Besides, arrangements may be made in State Legislatures for the 
establishment of Public Accounts Committee (PACs) . specifically 
for PRIs or for the accounts of PRIs to be submitted to PR 
Committees of the State Legislatures . State level committees, as in 
Andhra Pradesh, for the settlement of audit paras may also be 
considered. 
(vii) It may be useful to complement such institutional arrangements 
by legislating an ap propriate Fiscal Reponsibility Act for elected 
local authorities. 
(viii) Outsourcing of accounting by such measures as village 
panchayats being authorized to employ certified Chartered 
Accountants against standard contracts might be considered. 
(ix) The training of both officials and elected representatives in sound 
accounting and audit practices is a high priority. To this end, 
State Governments are invited to make full use of the Regional 
Training Institutes (RTIs) functioning under the aegis of the 
C&AG, in particular the RTI at Kolkata which has been declared 
a centre of excellence; as also of the Institute of Public Auditors 
of India (IPAI). Substantial additional funding from the Union 
Government to facilitate training is a high priority. 
(x) Those State Governments which have not as yet availed of the 
arrangements for bringing the C & AG into the exercise of 
accounting and audit, including the C&AG's Technical 
139 

RAJYA SABHA [16 August, 2005] 
Guidance and Supervision (TGS) Scheme for the PRIs, are 
invited to do so and the attention of all concerned is drawn to the 
publications of the Indian and Audit Accounts Department, in 
particular. 
(a) Auditing Standards for PRIs and Urban Local Bodies 
(b) Guidelines for Certification of Audit of Accounts of PRIs 
(c) Training module of Audit of Gram Panchayats 
(xi) Given the shortage of staff for undertaking formal accounts and 
audit work in the lakhs of Village Panchayats, thousands of 
Intermediate Panchayats and hundreds of Zilla Parishads around 
the country, it is essential that automation and computerization of 
accounts be undertaken with all deliberate speed and to this end 
software like the one beinq prepared by the Xavier Institute of 
Management, Bhubaneshwar for the Orissa State Government, 
for maintaining day-to-day accoun ts, which is expected to be 
ready by early 2004, be deployed as widely as possible 
everywhere. 
(xii) Social audit is an important complement to formal audit and for 
the sound and healthy development of Panchayati Raj, it is 
essential to establish a symbiotic relationship between social and 
formal audit. 
(xiii) Social audit must necessarily be undertaken at the level of the 
Gram Sabha but might also be undertaken at higher levels of the 
Panchayat Raj system, as in West Bengal. 
(xiv) For social audit to be effective and based on the best practices 
available in different States, consideration might be given to the 
preparation of Social Audit Policies for adoption by State 
Legislatures/Governments so as to provide a framework within 
which social audit is undertaken. Such Social Audit Policies may 
be targeted at facilitating popular participation in fighting 
corruption in Panchayats, as also complementing formal audit 
processes by quality assessment, ascertainment of preferences 
and the provision of choices. At the same time, Social Audit 
Policies may provide for institutional measures to prevent 
needless harassment. 
140 

[16 August, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
(xv) To ensure appropriate follow-up  to issues raised through social 
audit, legislative bodies and regulatory authorities might treat 
social audit resolutions on par with formal audit paras to ensure 
consideration and disposal within a time-bound frame work. 
(xvi) Given the critical importance of total disclosure of information 
for effective social audit, States  might consider passing Right to 
Information legislation, taki ng into account the legislation 
already on the books in such states as Rajasthan.

New oil pricing policy 
2287. SHRI DARA SINGH: Will th e Minister of PETROLEUM AND 
NATURAL GAS be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government are cware that petroleum products like petrol, 
diesel, LPG etc. are being sold to the consumers on the basis of import price, 
despite the fact that there is huge domestic investment in the refineries in the 
country; 
(b) if so, the names of beneficiaries of such huge domestic investment 
(refinery-wise); 
(c) the reasons for not percolating benefits down to the consumers in 
the country; 
(d) whether Government propose to formulate any new oil pricing to 
safeguard interest of consumers in the country; and 
(e) if so, the details thereof? 
THE MINISTER OF PETROLEUM AND NATURAL GAS (SHRI 
MANISHANKAR AIYAR): (a ) Sensitive petroleum products, including 
petrol, diesel, domestic LPG and PDS kerosene are not sold to consumers at 
the import parity price. In April, 200 2, with the intention of moving to 
market-determined pricing for petroleum products, Government announced 
the dismantling of the Administered  Pricing Mechanism (APM). In 
accordance with that decision, Public  Sector Oil Marketing Companies 
(OMCs) pay petroleum product's prices on an import parity basis to 
refineries, but full import parity prices are not realized from consumers of 
sensitive products like petrol, diesel, kerosene and domestic LPG. The 
difference is subsidized, partly by Government and largely by the oil sector. 
(b) There are eighteen (18)  refineries in the country including one in 
the private sector. The details are given in the statement (See below). 
145 

RAJYA SABHA [16 August, 2005] 
The setting up of these refineries has led to self-sufficiency in refining 
capacity and even substantial export capacity in the country 
(c) Do not arise in view of the substantial insulation of the consumers 
from the full impact of import parity  prices of crude oil and petroleum 
products. 
(d) and (e) Since June 2004, recognizing explicitly that international 
prices of crude oil and petroleum products decisively impact domestic prices, 
Government elucidated the principles which would govern its policy of 
containing the burden of increase in international prices on consumers of 
sensitive petroleum products. It was decided that the burden should be 
equitably shared by consumers, the Government and oil companies. 
Accordingly, Government pricing policy attempts to strike the right balance 
between the interests of the stake-holders, namely, consumers, OMCs and the 
Government No new pricing mechanism is under consideration as 
Government is already doing its utmost to safeguard the interests of 
consumers.

New irrigation projects 
2340. SHRI N.R. GOVINDARAJAR: Will the Minister, of 
WATER RESOURCES be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government propose to start any new irrigation projects to 
provide irrigation facilities to farmers; 
(b) if so, the extent to which the problem of farmers is likely to be 
mitigated as a result thereof; 
(c) whether Government have announ ced any package for farmers of 
Tamil Nadu; and 
(d) if so, the details thereof? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF WATER 
RESOURCES (SHRI JAI PRAKASH NARAYAN YADAV): (a) to (d) 
Irrigation being a State subject the irrigation projects are planned, formulated, 
funded and executed by the State Govern ments out of their own resources as 
per their priorities. The Central Government has not proposed new irrigation 
projects to provide irrigation facilities to farmers. However, a pilot scheme 
"National project for repair renovation and restoration of water bodies 
directly linked to Agriculture" has been approved by the Union Government 
in January, 2005 with a total outlay of Rs. 300 crore for the remaining period 
of Tenth Five Year Plan. The aims and objectives of the project are to restore 
and augment the storage capacity of wa ter bodies and to recover and extend 
their lost irrigation potential. The scheme envisages taking up pilot projects 
by the States in one or two district s. Ministry of Water Resources has 
approved projects in 16 districts of 9 States including Tamil Nadu. The 
schemes for restoration of 8 water bodies in the Sivagangai district and 38 
water bodies in the Villupuram district of Tamil Nadu estimated to cost Rs. 
10.594 crore have been approved. 
Study on underground water resources 
2341. SHRI C. RAMACHANDRAIAH: Will the Minister of WATER 
RESOURCES be pleased to state: 
202 

[16 August, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
(a) whether the Central Ground Water Board has found a vast 
subterranean water body of ground water in the belt around the upper Ganga 
canal; 
(b) if so, the details thereof; 
(c) whether any feasibility study has been conducted to check the 
quantity and quality of this vast underground water resources; and 
(d) if so, the details thereof and by when the work in this direction is 
likely to be started? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF WATER 
RESOURCES (SHRI JAI PRAKASH NARAYAN YADAV): (a) and (b) 
Based on ground water surveys and exploration carried out by the Central 
Ground Water Board (CGWB), an area of 250 sq. km. along Upper Ganga 
Canal has been identified which has potential for development of deeper 
aquifers. The identified area extends from Bhola (North of Jani) in Merrut 
district to Muradnagar in Ghaziabad district in Uttar Pradesh along the Upper 
Ganga Canal. The study has revealed that deeper aquifer between 100 and 
250 m. is unutilized and is separated from top aquifer by a thick clay bed 
varying in thickness from 18 to 55 m. The deeper aquifer is under high 
artesian head and ultimate discharge is in the saline belts in South West. 
(c) and (d) From the studies carried out by CGWB, it has been 
established that quality of deeper aquifer shows deterioration due to base 
exchange from the clay formation. Flow of ground water is very slow and 
over a very long period of time, salinity increases in southward directipn. The 
present quality in identified are is po table and aquifers have high hydraulic 
conductivity with tubewells capable of yielding upto 3000 litres per minute 
(LPM). 
Since the identified area is under the jurisdiction of Government of 
Uttar Pradesh, further action is to be taken by the State Government.

Expert report on Baglihar 
2342.    SHRI RAMA MUNI REDDY SIRIGIREDDY: 
SHRI K. RAMA MOHAN RAO: 
Will the Minister of WATER RESOURCES be pleased to state: 
(a) whether the neutral expert, Prof. Raymond Lafitte appointed to give 
opinion on Baghlihar has submitted his report; 
(b) whether it is a fact that Pakistan 's request to stop work on the 
project by India has been rejected; 
(c) what are the real technical problem s that are the bone of contention 
between India and Pakistan on Baglihar; and 
(d) the details of provisions that Paki stan claim are, being violated by 
India? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF WATER 
RESOURCES (SHRI JAI PRAKASH NARAYAN YADAV): (a) No, Sir. 
(b) Pakistan's request to India in this regard has been rejected. 
(c) Pakistan has basically objected to the extent of Pondage of water by 
India and the levels of the mechanisms for release of water viz. the gates and 
the intakes. Pakistan is of the view that the Pondage should be lesser and the 
gates & intakes should be located at higher levels than those provided in 
Indian design. India is however of the view that Pondage consistent with the 
permitted variations in the releases of water as stipulated in the Treaty and the 
levels of the gates and intakes consis tent with national and international 
practices at the highest levels consistent  with techno-economics as stipulated 
in the Treaty, have been provided. 
(d) Criteria (a), (c), (e) and (f) under Paragraph 8 of Annexure D to the 
Indus Water Treaty 1960, claimed by Paki stan to have been violated   by 
India are as follows: 
Criterion (a). The works themselves shall not be capable of raising 
artificially the water level in the Operating Pool above the Full Pondage 
Level specified in the design. 
204 

[16 August, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
Criterion (c) The maximum Pondage in the Operating Pool shall not 
exceed twice the Pondage required for Firm Power. 
Criterion (e) If the conditions at the site of a Plant make a gated 
spillway necessary, the botto m level of the gates in normal closed position 
shall be located at the highest level consistent with sound and economical 
design and satisfactory construction and operation of the works. 
Criterion (f) The intakes for the turbines shall be located at the highest 
level consistent with satisfactory and economical construction and operation 
of the Plant as a Run-of-River Pl ant and with customary and accepted 
practice of design for the designated range of the Plant's operation. 
Use of flood water for drinking or irrigation purpose 
†2343. SHRI DHARAM PAL SABHARWAL: 
SHRIMATI KUM KUM RAI: 
Will the Minister of WATER RESOURCES be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that several St ates face either flood or flood like 
situation every year while several othe r States face drough t or dearth of 
water; 
(b) if so, whether Government would make a policy to meet the 
shortage of water in drought hit States by bringing water from the States 
facing flood like situation; 
(c) whether it is also a fact that Go vernment are considering seriously 
to make proper use of the flood water for drinking or irrigation purpose; and 
(d) if so, the details thereof? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF WATER 
RESOURCES (SHRI JAI PRAKASH NARAYAN YADAV): (a) Yes, Sir. 
(b) The National Water Policy, 2002 emphasizes the need to transfer 
water from surplus areas to deficit ones . It states "water should be made 
available to water-short areas by transfer from other areas 
†Original notice of the question was received in Hindi. 
205 

RAJYA SABHA [16 August, 2005] 
including transfer from one river basin to another based on National 
Perspective Plan after taking into account requirements of the areas/ basins". 
(c) and (d) Yes, Sir. The Ministry of Water Resources and Central 
Water Commission formulated in 1980 a National Perspective Plan for Water 
Resources Development envisaging inter-basin transfer of water from surplus 
basins to deficit ones with a view to minimizing the regional imbalances and 
optimally utilize the available water re sources for conservation purposes like 
drinking, irrigation etc. National Perspective Plan comprises two components 
viz. (i) Himalayan rivers development and (ii) Peninsular rivers development. 
National Water Development Agency was set up in 1982 as a registered 
Society under MOWR to carry out detailed studies for National Perspective 
Plan. Based on various studies conducted, National Water Development 
Agency has identified 30 links for preparing Feasibility Reports. National 
Water Development Agency has completed feasibility reports for 14 links 
under Peninsular Development Component and two links under Himalayan 
Rivers Development Component.

The Supreme Court on 12th August, 2005, through a judgement, allows 
full freedom to the management of t he self-financing private professional 
educational institutions to take all t he students by themselves, denying the 
Government's quota totally. This is against all principles of social justice and, if 
this judgement is implemented, the poor students of all communities will not be 
able to get admission if self-financing educational institutions. The only away 
out from the judgement seems to me is to  have a Central legislation on self-
financing professional educational inst itutions restoring the 50 per cent 
Government quota and making it applicabl e to all self-financed professional 
institutions in the country . And, the fee should be collected as prescribed by 
the Government. 
So, I urge upon the Government of I ndia to either immediately introduce 
a Bill, in this Session itself, or, immediately take steps to issue an Ordinance 
so that the anxiety of the entire student-community is solved. Thank you.

SHRI P. CHIDAMBARAM: Sir, no one is  happy that the Bihar Budget is 
being discussed in this House and in the Lok Sabha. Certainly, I am not happy. If 
this situation has come to pass, it is because of the fractur ed mandate delivered 
by the people of Bihar and the inability of  the political parties in Bihar to put 
together a Government. No one in the Central Government can be blamed for 
that. You can blame the Central Government for acting or not acting 
270 

[16 August, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
in a particular manner after a situati on has arisen in Bihar. But that debate 
took place in this House, that debat e has been concluded. It is certainly no 
part of my responsibilities to reopen t hat debate. All I can hope for is the 
passion, the concern and the reason brought to bear on this debate by the 
hon. Members from Bihar should, I hope, help them convince the people of 
Bihar to elect a Government with a work ing majority so that that Government 
can run for five years. 
Sir, the constant refrain has been that money is a problem for Bihar. I 
think, it is time that we laid this ghost to rest. Money has not been a constraint 
in the case of Bihar. Look at the Tw elfth Finance Commission. Bihar will get 
its share of Central taxes, that is a Constitutional mandate and a 
Constitutional provision. No one can deny Bihar one rupee share in the 
Central taxes to which it is  entitled. It is a matter of simple calculation. Let us 
look at grants. The Twelfth Finance Commission has been generous to Bihar. 
There are grants for Panchayati-Raj institutions, grants for urban local bodies, 
grants for calamity relief. Bihar is one among the handful of States chosen by 
the Twelfth Finance Commission for a special grant under education and 
health. 
Under education, while the normal expenditure in five years, beginning 
2005-06 is expected to be about Rs. 20, 410 crores, the grants-in-aid to Bihar 
is Rs. 2,683 crores. Under health, while the normal expenditure for five years 
beginning 2005-06 is Rs. 3,150 crores, the grants-in-aid is Rs. 1,819 crores. 
There are grants for maintenance of forest, there are grants for heritage 
conservation. State-SpecifiQ Need grants for Bihar is Rs. 400 crores. So, I do 
not think money is a constraint. What is a constraint is, I think, better 
administration, better governance, and ac countability for every rupee that is 
spent. 
Sir, in 2005-06 Budget which I pr esent, the outlays have been vastly 
increased over the Revised Estimates of  2004-05. For roads, the increase in 
outlay is 104 per cent, for health it is 45 per cent, for drinking water it is 60 per 
cent, for rural development it is 23.5 per cent, for backward districts 
development under Rashtriya Shram Vikas Yojana it is 205 per cent, for 
urban development it is 104 per cent, fo r irrigation and flood control it is 21.8 
per cent, and agriculture it is 12.5 per cent. 
Power is a constraint. It is true that Bihar has done very poorly so far as 
power is concerned. Bihar's own generation is only about

50 MW. The Central sector allocation to Bihar averages about 700 MW per 
month. The average demand in the St ate is 990 MW and the peak hours 
demand is 1440 MW. Now these four figures give the story of Bihar's power 
sector. National per capita consumption of power is 566 KW/Hours whereas 
Bihar's per capita is only 74 KW/Hours. What I find painful is finger pointing. 
People point fingers to each other. But so meone said that for each finger that 
is pointed, I think, three fingers are pointing to oneself. Everybody has been in 
power in Bihar at some time or the othe r. Bihar's woes did not start in March 
2005; Bihar's woes did not start after President's rule was imposed. Bihar has 
had a history of good governance and poor governance. When Bihar had good 
governance, Bihar was held up as a model for many States. When Bihar had 
poor governance, Bihar and the people of Bihar paid a price. It is not my 
business to fix responsibility. That is the business of the people of Bihar. Nor is 
it my business to find fault. My busi ness is to ensure that the Budget is 
passed, money is provided, and some wo rk is undertaken in the few months 
that we hold responsibility for the Governance of Bihar. Sir, I do not want to go 
into great detail about the numbers; numbers are there in the Budget papers. 
In education, the total outlay in the current year is Rs. 3680 crores. In the 
health sector, the outlay has been increased  from Rs. 783 crores last year to 
Rs. 1142 crores in the current year. Expenditure in the first quarter—April, May 
and June - as I told the Lok Sabha, has been rather low. When this was 
brought to my notice, I have written to  the Governor pointing out that Plan 
expenditure has been very low, less than five per cent in the first quarter and 
this must be considerably and quickly stepped up. Part of the reason is 
uncertainty that hovers over Bihar and the administration. We were not sure 
whether a Government would be formed;  we were not sure whether the 
President's Rule would come to an end. But the President's Rule had to be 
imposed and then the President's Rule had to be extended, I think, 
administration is now geared up to dischar ge its duties. I am told that while up 
to June the expenditure has been only five per cent, in July there has been a 
sharp increase in expenditure and that up to July the Plan expenditure may 
have increased up to 9 per cent. 
Sir, a question was asked about the projects in pipeline in the power 
sector. Under the Rashtriya Shramvikas Yojana a detailed project report is 
being prepared for Phase-ll, the st rengthening of transmission line and 
construction of sub-stations in S outh Bihar. Also for rehabilitation and 
modernisation, proposals worth Rs. 5.50 crores

The Hindu Succession (Amendment) Bill, 2004 
THE MINISTER OF LAW AND JUSTICE (SHRI H.R. BHARDWAJ): Sir I 
beg to move: 
That the Bill further to amend the Hindu Succession Act, 1956, be 
taken into consideration. 
Sir, I have the pleasure to commend the Hindu Succession 
(Amendment) Bill, 2004, for consideration of this august House. 
The National Common Minimum Programme of our Government Inter 
alia seeks to give complete legal equality for women in all spheres a practical 
reality, especially by removing discriminative legislation and by enacting a new 
legislation that gives equal rights of ownership of assets like houses and land. 
Sir, you are aware that Article 14 and 15 of our Constitution guarantees 
equality before laws and gender equality. Article 15 of the Convention on the 
Elimination of All forms of Discrim ination Against Women adopted by the 
United Nations General assembly on 18th December, 1979 clearly mandates 
that the State shall accord  to women equality with men before law and in all 
civil matters. The Universal Declaration of Human Rights also guarantees 
substantial equal justice to women. 
Sir, in this perspective, we have brought the Hindu Succession 
(Amendment) Bill, 2004 before this au gust House on 20th December, 2004. 
The Bill was referred to the Parlia mentary Standing Committee, and, I am 
happy to inform this august House that the Committee has returned the Bill 
with certain recommendations. 
Sir, we are all aware that the Hin du law was consolidated in the 50s 
when the Hindu Marriage Act, 1955, the Hindu Adoption and Maintenance Act, 
1956, the Hindu Succession Act, 1956 and the Hindu Minority and 
Guardianship Act, 1956 were adopted. We  generally call these pieces of 
legislations, the Hindu Code as the legislation was originally moved as the 
Hindu code Bill. 
292 

[16 August, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
After this, there was a demand to confer equality to women in the matter 
of coparcenary property. Section 6 of the Hindu succession Act deals with the 
devolution of interest in coparcenar y property. The provision clearly 
discriminates daughters, as they are not coparceners like the sons. This 
provision has been identified by the La w Commission of India as one of the 
discriminative provisions violating articl es 14 and 15 of the Constitution. The 
Commission made a suo motu study of the discriminative provisions of the 
Hindu Succession Act and presented its 17 4th Report on "Property Rights of 
Women: Proposed reform; under the Hindu Law" (may, 2000) to the Central 
Government. The Government considered the said Report in consultation with 
the State Governments and decided to give  equal right to daughter in Hindu 
joint family property governed by the Mitakshara law. In this connection, I 
would like to inform this august House that several States have already made 
local amendments to the Act. These are:- I) The Hindu Succession (Andhra 
Pradesh Amendment) Act, 1986; ii) The Hindu Succession (Tamil Nadu 
Amendment) Act, 1990; iii) The Hindu Succession (Karnataka Amendment) 
Act, 1994; iv) The Hindu Succession (Maharashtra Amendment) Act, 1994; 
and, by the Kerala Joint Hindu Family System (Abolition) Act, 1974, the State 
of Kerala has totally abolished the right by birth of males and put an end to the 
joint Hindu family system instead of tinkering with the coparcenary. Sir this has 
to be improved further and now the present law makes certain provisions. The 
benefit of the proposed new secsion relating to devolution of interest in 
coparcenary property is one item, and, declaring daughters also as 
coparceners by birth is proposed to be extended to married daughters as well 
subject to the condition that it shall no t affect or invalidate any disposition or 
alienation including any partition or te stamentary disposition of property which 
has taken place before the introduction of this Bill in Rajya Sabha on 20th 
December, 2004. 
It has been represented that there is a generational difference of depth 
of successors of male and female. It is now proposed fo remove this disparity 
by putting the same depth of a generation in Class One of the heirs. The 
Standing Committee has recommended omi ssion of section 24, which deals 
with prevention of certain widows from inhering property of the interstate if she 
gets remarried as there 
293 

RAJYA SABHA [16 August, 2005] 
is no corresponding disability to widowers. It is proposed to amend this 
section. 
Sir, I think, these are very progressi ve measures and, I hope, there will 
be no difficulty for this hon. House to pass this Bill. With these words, I 
commend this Bill for the consideration of the House. 
The question was proposed.

SHRIMATI N.P. DURGA (Andhra Prades h): Mr. Deputy Chairman, Sir, I 
rise to speak on the Hindu Succession (Amendment) Bill, placed before the 
House for its consideration by the hon. Minister. The subject is dearer to me 
becuase it is our late beloved leader and former Chief Minister of A.P., Shri 
NT. Rama Rao, who for the first time in India, gave women equal share in 
property rights in the St ate of A.P but, whatever changes proposed in the 
present Bill are only cosmetic in nature and are in no way help the women in 
India. I give my justification to this st atement in due course of my speech. As 
has been pointed out in the 174th Report of  the Law Commission it is true that 
discrimination against women is so perv asive that it sometimes surface on a 
bare perusal of law made by this very Legislature. And, it is particularly so 
when it comes to laws governing the inheritance or succession of property 
amongst the members of the Joint Hindu Family. Sir, it is not only Manu who 
advocated women subordination, but even  our legislature and the judiciary 
made women dependent and subservient to  man - when she is child, on her 
father; as a wife, on her husband; and in  old age, on the son-for everything. 
We have been working on the issue of amelioration of women's position in 
society over the last about 80 year s, when the first the Hindu Law of 
Inheritance Act 1929, was passed, t hen, in 1937, through Hindu Women's 
Right to Property Act, and then in 1956 and so many amendments to it. But, 
nothing positive has come out. The proposed Bill is, of course, to some extent, 
important towards gender equality and abo lition of the patrilineal system of 
inheritance prevailing among Hindus. But, however, not only to my mind but 
almost all the women organizations , the proposed changes are not 
comprehensive enough and women will still be subjected to unequal property 
rights in many areas. The other poin t is, the proposed Amendments to the 
Mitakshara Joint Family Property laws making women equal coparceners are

sought to be made applicable only to women who are not married at the time 
this law is passed and is thus patent ly unjust because you are denying this 
right to women who have already married. It is not out of place to mention 
here that A. P. is the first State in the country  which made daughter a 
coparcencer of the Joint Hindu Family. So, I request to have some cut off date 
for this. 
I wish to have reply from the hon. Minister on a point. Is it not a fact that 
during the enactment of Dowry Prohib ition Act, women organizations have 
demanded for abolition of Joint Family Sy stem? At that time, it was assured 
that when the Hindu Succession Act would be amended this request would be 
considered. But, now you have done nothing on this. So, in a sense, the 
proposed amendment does not go far enough. 
Through substitution of Section 6 with a new one and deleting Section 
23, you are giving a little solace to women but, there are so many Sections 
which are blatantly discriminate against women in this country and are needed 
amendments. I would like to know why th e Minister's attention has not been 
drawn towards these sections? The most important Section, which is used to 
deny property right to women in agricultu ral land is Section 4(2) of the Hindu 
Succession Act. The courts have upheld the State Land Reform Acts relating 
to devolution of tenancy right even though these do not allow women to inherit 
these tenancies. Some courts have furt her interpreted the term devolution of 
tenancy rights comprehensively to include devolution of tenure holder's right 
and have thus also denied women ownership rights over agricultural land. 
Thus, even laws meant for land reform and to enforce ceiling have resulted it 
denying to women equal rights over land and a chance to. improve her 
disempowerment. Even responding to the questionnaire of the Law 
Commission, 81 per cent of the resp ondents favoured bringing gender 
equality in the heritance of agricultura l land. But, the Ministry has done 
nothing in this regard. 
The next point I wish to deal with is with regard to Section 30 eft the Act, 
which allows any Hindu to dispose of his property, including his share in the 
joint family property, by will. Is the Mi nister not aware that this very Section 
can, and has been, used to disinherit  women? Has it not been recommended

to know whether the Ministry

has taken any steps in this regard. If yes, the details may be given. I would

Extension of SEZ facilities 
*321. SHRI K. RAMA MOHANA RAO: Will the Minister of COMMERCE AND 
INDUSTRY be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that Indian apparel Export Units are demanding for extending 
SEZ facilities to their units set up outside SEZ; 
(b) if so, the details thereof; 
(c) whether it is also a fact that the Government of Andhra Pradesh has requested 
for opening up of SEZ; and 
(d) if so, the details of the request and the action that has been contemplated on that? 
THE MINISTER OF COMMERCE AND INDUSTRY (SHRI KAMAL 
NATH): (a) and (b) Suggestions have been received for extending facilities such as 
exemption from income tax as available to units in SEZ to apparel export units located 
outside the SEZ. 
(c) and (d) On the basis of proposals received through the Government of Andhra 
Pradesh, approval has been given for setting up of 2 Special Economic Zones in 
Visakhapatnam and Kakinada. The Zone at visakhapatnam is proposed to be 
developed by AP Industrial Infrastructure Corporation Limited while that at Kakinada by the 
Kakinada SEZ Private Limited. 
SHRI K. RAMA MOHANA RAO: Sir, the Minister has said that the Indian apparel 
export units have been demanding income-tax exemptions as are available to the units in 
SEZ. Not only income-tax exemptions, but they are also demanding duty-free imports or 
domestic procurement of goods operating outside SEZs apart from other things. 
Therefore, in my 

RAJYASABHA [17 August, 2005] 
first supplementary, I would like to know from the hon. Minister to what 
extent he has succeeded in giving them facilities demanded by the Indian apparel 
export units. May I know whether the Minister can give any time limit, by 
which the SEZs in Visakhapatnam and Kakinada become operational? 
SHRI KAMAL NATH: Sir, the second part first that the Andhra Pradesh 
Industrial Development Corporation has to develop these. They have been 
giving the approval; and the other one in Kakinada is a private party. This is 
really for the State Government to drive it, and, to the extent of the regulatory 
framework, which involves the Stat e Government, where the approval is 
concerned, that has already been given. So, if there is a concern regarding SEZs 
or the developers of the SEZs find any difficulty or need any clarification, the 
Central Government would act immediately. 
The other question relates to apparel units or textile units which have been 
demanding some of the facilities of the SEZs. Sir, the SEZ is a regime of its 
own, it is as per the Act passed by Parliament, by this august House and there is a 
criterion to be an SEZ. We cannot have proliferation of SEZs because SEZ 
envisages a lot of freedom from the regulato.ry framework; it provides more or 
less autonomous structure where customs and other fiscal facilities are 
concerned. So, there have been demands that those who are exporting should 
get some facilities of the SEZs; and to give them level playing field. We cannot 
have a thing called virtual SEZ. Either there is a SEZ or there is no SEZ. SEZ 
is area specific. 
SHRI K. RAMA MOHANA RAO: Sir, in my second supplementary, I 
would like to know from the hon. Minister whether it is true that there were 
some policy changes made by the Government in the month of September, 
2004 to give further boost to the units set up by SEZ. If, 'yes', what impact does 
the policy changes have on the export of goods from SEZs in the first half of 
this fiscal? May I know whether these changes are going to be made 
applicable to the units outside SEZs? If not, the reasons may be given.

hon. Members are aware, the SEZs fi rst worked under the administrative 
control, worked outside the domain of legal framework. After passing of the 
SEZ Bill by the Parliament, now it is governed under the Act. All the facilities to 
give it a regime of stability.are contained in the

framework various facilities and concessions so that the investors would have 
confidence.That being done so, now the SEZ Act, having been passed by both 
the Houses of Parliament, having been notified, is now operational. So, there is

SHRI JAIRAM RAMESH: Sir, the hon. Minister just said that he is against 
the proliferation of SEZs. But, I understand that there are proposals for around 56

advisory services on maintenance of the young tea plantations are being extended 
to the tea growers through the extension wing of Tea Research Association.

Children killed by army ambush in J&K 
*327.    SHRI PRAMOD MAHAJAN: 
SHRIMATI SUSHMA SWARAJ: 
Will the Minister of DEFENCE be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government are aware that  an army ambush killed three 
innocent children in J&K; and 
(b) if so, what steps Government are taking so that such mistakes do not 
happen in future? 
THE MINISTER OF DEFENCE (SHRI PRANAB MUKHERJEE): (a) and 
(b) In the light of the recent spurt in infiltration attempts in the State of Jammu and 
Kashmir (J&K), the Army troops have been put on high alert. On the night of 
23rd/24th July, 2005, the Army laid an ambush near Bangargund (near Vilgam 
in Kupwara District in North Kashmir). At about 01.55 hours, the ambush party 
noticed a movement of three to four persons. As they approached the ambush 
site, the Junior Commissioned Officer (JCO) challenged the group, asking them 
to identify themselves. The challenged persons started running in various 
directions. They were again warned to stop. However, when they did not heed 
to the warning, the JCO act ivated the mine, that had been placed to cover the 
ambush site. On hearing the blast and subsequent cries of wounded persons, the 
JCO and two other Army personnel moved ahead to investigate. The search 
of the ambush site revealed two fatal and two non-fatal civilian casualties. The 
injured were immediately provided first aid and evacuated to a Field Ambulance. 
One of the injured later succumbed to injuries. On further investigation, it was 
revealed that the casualties were civilians aged between 15 to 18 years and 
residents of Bangargund village. 
31 

RAJYA SABHA [17 August, 2005] 
The area of current incident adjoins the Rajwar forest, which is a traditional 
infiltration route from Keran Sector, leading to the areas in Kupwara region. On 
numerous occasions, the Army had requested the villagers to restrict their movement at 
night, and in case of emergencies, the persons moving were to carry 
lanterns/torches. 
However, the incident has been deeply regretted by the Army. Compensation of 
Rs. three lakhs each to the dead and Rs. two lakhs to the injured civilian has been paid. It is 
pertinent to mention that, the troops deployed in J&K are in a state of perpetual high 
alert, in view of the recent spurt in infiltration attempts by terrorists. To avoid 
repetition of incidents of collateral damage due to mistaken identity, the local population has 
been once again cautioned to strictly follow the instructions under Section 144 and in 
case of emergenices, carry lanterns/torches at night. The Army troops, in turn have been 
sensitized to- exercise restraint and use discretion during conduct of counter terrorist 
operations.

Programmes and schemes to increase the production, quality, productivity 
and the competitiveness of the domestic silk industry. 
• Research and Development efforts of Central Silk Board have been 
stepped up to improve quantity and productivity of sericulture, by 
evolution of more productive and stress tolerant breeds and hybrids of 
mulberry and non-mulberry food plants and silkworms; and 
development of low cost reeling and processing technologies in silk; 
• Seed Support and Technical Assistance is being given by the Central 
Silk Board to State Governments, farmers and reelers by maintenance 
of parent races and basic seed, supply of commercial seed, and 
augmentation of grainage facilities for production of disease free high 
yielding and drought resistant seeds;

Sponsored and Central sector schemes to strengthen farm infrastructure, 
increase area under sericulture, up grade reeling facilities, improve

systems; 
• Low cost and productivity enhancing technologies developed by the 
Central Silk Board are being popula rized through Central assistance to 
beneficiaries, training to the States' extension machinery and 
beneficiaries, organizing of various awareness programmes, etc.;

point less than applicable bank rate, under the Technological 
Upgradation Fund Scheme (TUFS) for the textiles sector is available inter

• Supply chain issues between the farm ers, raw silk producers and the 
weavers are being addressed by ad vocating contract farming models, 
price linked grading, etc. 
• Establishing quality certification systems for silkworm seeds, cocoons, 
yarn and fabric.

programmes;

abroad, market research and surveys, etc.

RAJYA SABHA [17 August, 2005] 
T&D losses of MSEB 
*339. SHRI VIJAY J. DARDA: Will the Minister of POWER be pleased to 
state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that in MSEB (Maharashtra State Electricity Board) 
there has been nearly 40 per cent Transmission and Distribution losses and it has 
resulted into a debt of over Rs. 5,000 crore to MSEBT; 
(b) if so, what are the r easons for this huge Transmission and Distribution 
losses and what steps have been taken to ensure that these are brought to the 
minimum nationally acceptable limit; and 
(c) what is the Union Power Ministry's norms in this regard and what 
guidelines are issued to ensure that St ate Electricity Board keep within this 
norm? 
THE MINISTER OF POWER (SHRI P.M. SAYEED): (a) As informed by 
Maharashtra State Electricity Board [p resently known as Maharashtra State 
Electricity Distribution Company Ltd. (MSEDCL)] the transmission and 
distribution (T&D) losses for the year 2004-05 have been estimated at 35.28%. 
This loss includes Technical loss and Non-technical (commercial) loss. 
Although, it is difficult to segregate Technical & Non-Technical (commercial) 
loss, MSEDCL has stated that they are likely to face a shortfall of revenue of 
Rs.2500 crores assuming the technical losses to be about 20% and non-
technical to be 15.28% (10,280 MU of energy). 
(b) In MSEDCL, most of the power is generated by Thermal Power Plants, 
which are located in Eastern part (Vidarbha area) of Maharashtra. The demand 
for electrical power is, however, c oncentrated in central and western 
Maharashtra. All the power generated by the thermal plants is, therefore, 
required to be transmitted to Western Maharashtra over a distance of 600-650 
kms. This results in high losses in Transmission network. Similarly while 
distributing the power to the consumers through its network there is a loss due 
to technical reasons (i.e. heating of conductors etc.) Over a period of time, theft 
of electricity by direct hooking on the LT Lines and tampering of meters etc. have 
been on the rise. The above reasons mainly contribute towards the higher level 
of T&D loss in MSEDCL. 
44 

[17 August, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
The steps initiated by MSEDCL to reduce the T&D losses are:— 
(i) Erection of new 33/11 KV sub-stations, HT Lines, distribution 
transformers under APDRP Scheme, so as to reduce the overloading at 
all levels thus reducing the technical losses. 
(ii) Providing capacitors on Distribution Transformers in 20 Districts, 
(iii) Distribution Transformer Metering and Energy Accounting, 
(iv) Monitoring the losses in MIDC areas and Express Feeders. 
(v) Detection of theft through flying squads. 
(vi) Establishment of six dedicated po lice stations and three special courts 
for prevention/detection of theft cases and expeditious finalization of 
punishments. 
(vii) High Voltage Distribution System (HVDS) Scheme for theft prone areas being 
implemented to improve HT/LT ratio and thereby reduce the losses. 
(viii) Separate feeders for Gaothans (Habitations) being planned for 4500 
feeders, which will help reduce HT losses. 
(ix) Procurement of distribution transformers having lesser no load losses 
and full load losses. 
(x) System Improvement schemes for establishment of 60 new 33/11 KV 
sub-stations. 
(c). The Government of India ha s launched the Accelerated Power 
Development and Reforms Programme (APDRP) with the objective of 
reducing Aggregate Technical and Commercial Losses (AT&C) to a level of 15% 
improving quality of supply of power, increasing revenue collection and 
improving consumer satisfaction. APDRP has been put in place as instrument 
to leverage distribution reforms in the States. Priority is given to projects from 
those States who commit themselves to a time-bound programme of reforms 
as elaborated in the Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) and 
Memorandum of Agreement (MoA). Signing of the above documents by the 
State Governments/SEBs/Utilities is a pre-requisite for releasing funds under 
APDRP.

Amendment to the protection of Human Rights Act 
*340.   SHRI KALRAJ MISHRA: 
SHRI TARLOCHAN SINGH: Will the Minister of 
HOME AFFAIRS be pleased to state: 
(a) whether the National Human Rights Commission had demanded an 
amendment to the Protection of Human Rights Act, observing that "good 
governance would remain an unfulfilled dream"; 
(b) if so, in what context and background this observation and demand was 
made and what is the nature and substance of the amendment sought; and 
(c) the Government's response thereto? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HOME AFFAIRS 
(SHRI SHRI PRAKASH JAISWAL): (a) to (c) The National Human Rights 
Commission (NHRC) has proposed several amendments to the Protection of 
Human Rights Act, 1993. The Amendments suggested by the NHRC are 
sensitive in nature and seek to alter the scope and character of the functioning 
of the human rights institutions established under the provisions of the PHR 
Act, 1993. The amendments, inter-alia, seek to empower the NHRC to enquire 
into the allegations of violations of human rights by the Armed Forces as against 
the special procedure prescribed under the Act in such cases, to take 
cognizance of and inquire into allegations of violation of human rights 
notwithstanding the cognizance thereof taken by any other Commission, except 
a Commission appointed under the Commission of Inquiries Act, 1952, 
constitution of Human Rights Courts mandated to dispose off cases within a time 
limit of three months, enabling the Commission to publish its Annual Reports or 
Sepcial Report on expiry of a period of  three months of its receipt in the 
Government even if the Report has not  been placed in Parliament/State 
Legislatures etc. These amendments are being examined keeping in view 
various factors like the objectives of  the Protection of Human Rights Act, 
1993, the role and character of the human rights institutions provided for under 
the Act etc.

† 2353. SHRI HARISH RAWAT: Will the Minister of COMMERCE AND 
INDUSTRY be pleased to state: 
(a) whether there is any special scheme for giving incentives to the States which 
produce tea suitable for exports; 
(b) the details of assistance being provided to various States under this scheme; 
(c) whether Uttaranchal has sent any proposal for special assistance for revival of old 
areas of tea production and extension of new areas; and 
(d) if so, the details thereof? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF COMMERCE AND 
INDUSTRY (SHRI E.V.K.S. ELANGOVAN): (a) and (b) A new scheme has been 
approved by the Government for providing incentive to the tea producers for producing 
more orthodox teas. This scheme, which became effective from 1st January, 2005 will 
remain in force upto 31st March, 2007. The total outlay earmarked for the schemers 
Rs. 65 crores. 
The scheme is expected to help the industry in changing the product mix to suit the 
demands of the export market. India is essentially a CTC tea producer whereas there is 
greater demand for orthodox tea in the international market. In order to induce the 
producers to produce more orthodox teas, incentive will be given at the rate of Rs. 3 per 
kg for leaf grades and Rs. 2 per kg. for dust grade orthodox teas. An additional subsidy 
at the rate of Rs. 2 per kg. will be provided for the incremental 
volume of orthodox tea produced.

Targets for Indo-Pak trade after SAFTA 
2356. SHRIVI JAY J. DARDA: Will th e Minister of COMMERCE AND 
INDUSTRY be pleased to state: 
(a) what targets have been fixed, over the existing one, the bilateral trade 
between India and Pakistan after introduction of South Asian Free Trade Area 
(SAFTA) from January 1, 2006. 
(b) whether wheat export to Pakistan is also be included over and above the 600 
items which Pakistan is presently importing from India; and 
(c) as Pakistan is presently importing  wheat from Russia, US, etc. on 
comparatively high price, will Government be initiating negotiations in this 
regard? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF COMMERCE AND 
INDUSTRY (SHRI E.V.K.S. ELANGOVAN): (a) During 2004-05, exports 
from India to Pakistan was valued at US $ 505 million as compared to US $ 
287 million during 2003-04 registering an increase of 76 per cent. During 
2004-05, imports from Pakistan into India was valued at US-$95 million as 
compared to US $ 58 million during 2003-04 showing an increase of 64 per 
cent. 
Under South Asian Free Trade Area Agreement (SAFTA) a phased tariff 
liberalization programme is envisaged. In two years, non-Least Developed 
Contracting States (India, Pakistan and Sri Lanka) will bring down tariffs to 
20% while Least Developed Contracting States 
59 

RAJYA SABHA [17 August, 2005] 
(Bangladesh, Bhutan, Maldives and Nepal) will bring them down to 30%. Non-LDCS will 
then bring down tariffs from 20% to 0-5% in 5 years, while LDCS will do so in 8 years. 
SAFTA is expected to be fully operationalised by 2016. No targets have been fixed for the 
bilateral trade between India and Pakistan after introduction of SAFTA from January 1, 
2006. 
(b) No, Sir. Pakistan has so far allowed 771 items for imports into 
Pakistan from India which do not include wheat. 
(c) During the meeting of two Commerce Ministers of India and Pakistan 
on the sidelines of G-20 Meeting held in March, 2005, India had raised 
the issue of import of wheat by Pakistan from other countries at 
comparatively higher prices and had requested to source the same from 
India at competitive price. The Commerce Minister of Pakistan, while 
noting this request, said that during the last financial year, Pakistan 
produced surplus wheat and, therefore, did not require to import wheat 
from any source.

Community;

THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF COMMERCE AND

One time package for tea and coffee/sectors 
2373.   DR. T. SUBBARAMI REDDY: 
SHRIMATI JAMANA DEVI BARUPAL: 
Will the Minister of COMMERCE AND INDUSTRY be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Union Government has approved one time package for tea 
industry and also coffee sectors; 
(b) whether these two schemes of tea and coffee will be implemented by Tea 
Board during the remaining period of Tenth Five Year Plan; 
(c) whether on coffee package CCEA has approved equal sharing of total 
interest burden on special coffee term loans during 3 year moratorium period of 
Rs. 287.1 crore amongst the banks; and 
(d) if so, to what extent this decision will help tea and coffee growers? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF COMMERCE AND 
INDUSTRY (SHRI E.V.K.S. ELANGOVAN): (a) to (d) In order to help the tea 
and coffee growers, the Government has recently approved the two packages 
for tea and coffee sectors. 
Package for tea Sector 
The Tea Board would implement the following two schemes during the 
Tenth Plan period, with an outlay of Rs. 93 crores with the funds to be made 
available from the special fund created wi th collections of additional duty of 
excise on tea. 
(i) Grant of subsidy for production of orthodox tea @ Rs.3 per kg for leaf 
grades and Rs 2 per kg for dust grades for existing levels of production with 
additional incentive @ Rsr 2 per kg for the incremental volume over the 
previous year from 1st January 2005 to 31st march 2007 with an outlay of 
Rs. 65 crores. 
(ii) Meeting the actual deficits of  the two research and Development 
Institutions viz. Tea Research Association (TRA) at Tocklai (Assam) and United 
Planters'Association for Southern India-Tea Research Foundation (UPASI-
TRF), Tamil Nadu for a period of five years with effect from 2004-05 subject 
to the maximum of 80% of the expenditure on already agreed items of 
expenditure, of which 49% would be met from the normal Plan outlay of the Tea 
Board and the balance from the special fund. The 
81 

RAJYA SABHA [17 August, 2005] 
outlay for this scheme for a period of five years from 2004-05 i.e from 2004-05 to 
2008-09 would be Rs. 28 crores. 
Package for coffee sector 
With a view to provide relief to coffee growers, Government has approved a 
special relief package to revive coffee sector which envisages the following:- 
(i) Sharing equally the total interest burden on Special Coffee Term  Loan (SCTL) 
during the three year moratorium period of Rs. 287.10 crores amongst the banks, the 
Government and the grower loanees to the extent of one third each. The Government 
Subsidy will be released only after growers had paid their share in full by the end of 
June 2005. 
(ii) To request the banks to lower the interest rates charged on SCTL from the existing 
11% to 9% or rate applicable to agriculture sector whichever is lower, during the 
remaining repayment period of SCTL loans. 
(iii) Writing off coffee developmental loans along with interest amounting to around Rs.24 
crore, due from the Coffee Board to the Government of India. The Coffee Board will 
in turn waive the old developmental loans amounting to around Rs.64.59 crore 
extended by the Board to the coffee growers (below 10 hectares) only. 
(iv) Providing the interest subsidy scheme on working capital loans for small growers 
(below 10 ha) at the rate of 5% and for large growers at rate of 3% for the remaining 
years of the Tenth Plan. However, this subsidy would be reduced by 1% for a 
period of 3 years in the case of those growers who receive the benefit of reduced 
interest burden on SCTL during the moratorium period. 
The above packages are expected to improve tea production and reduce the debt burden 
of coffee growers.

Growth Centre Scheme 
2375.     SHRI JANARADAN DWIVEDI: 
SHRI MOTILAL VORA: 
Will the Minister of COMMERCE AND INDUSTRY be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that there was a Growth Centre Scheme of 
Government; 
(b) if so, what is the status of that scheme and its achievements; and 
(c) what steps Government is taking to expedite the delivery mechanisms 
of all its Central infrastructural schemes? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTERY OF COMMERCE 
AND INDUSTRY (SHRI E.V.K.S.ELANGOVAN) (a) Yes, Sir. 
(b) With a view to promote industrialisation of backward areas in the 
country, the Government of India, in June 1988, had announced the Growth 
Centre Scheme which became operational from 1991 under which 71 Growth 
Centres were proposed to be set up throughout the country with basic 
infrastructure facilities such as powe r, water, telecommunications and 
banking to enable them to attract investment. These have been allocated 
amongst States on the basis of a combined criteria of area, population and 
extent of industrial backwardness. The Central Government assists the State 
Governments by contributing upto Rs. 10 crore by way of equity for each 
growth centre. The balance funds are to be raised by the State Governments 
and their agencies who implement the project. The amount of Central 
assistance has been increased to Rs. 15  crore for each growth centre in the 
North-Eastern Region, Himachal Prad esh, Uttranchal, Jammu & Kashmiri 
Sikkim. Out of 71 growth centres, 64 have acquired land for the project. 47 
growth centres have become functional, where allotment of plots has 
commenced. Under the scheme full central assistance has been released to 26 
growth centres. Industrial activity has commenced in 32 growth centres, 1074 
units have been establised, Rs. 10608.788 crore have been invested by the 
entrepreneurs and 36887 persons have got employment at various growth 
centres. Total amount released by the State Governments and their agencies is 
Rs. 816.5176 crore and the total 
84

Central released is Rs.522.56 crore. Total expenditure incurred on the growth 
centres project is Rs.1235.0251 crore. 
(c) For Centrally sponsored schemes, an institutionalised monitoring 
mechanism has been put in place which comprises constitution of a State Level 
Committee in each State to oversee and review the progress on quarterly basis 
and furnish the same to Ministry along -with utilisation certificate of the central 
assistance released. The progress of the scheme is reviewed in the Ministry on the 
basis of these reports. It is followed by suitable interaction with the State Governments 
in order to expedite the progress.

most of the States in the Country. Some States have revised their Police Act.

Commission namely the National Police Commission under the Chairmanship 
of Shri Dharam Vira in November, 1977. The Commission subm itted eight 
reports during the period February, 1979 to May 1981 with a number of 
recommendations, which were primarily to be implemented by the State 
Governments. The Reports of the Commission were therefore sent to all the 
State Governments/Union Territory Administrations for consideration and 
implementation. Subsequently, Padmanabhaiah Committee and Malimath 
Committee submitted their reports in 2000 & 2003 which touched upon 
various facets of Police functioning. 
(d) and (e) Yes, Sir. A public interest litigation filed by Shri Prakash Singh 
& Others is pending in the Supreme Court soliciting directions to the Central 
and State Governments with regard to implementation of various 
recommendations of the National Police Commission particularly in the matter 
of selection and fixity of tenure of Director General of Police, formation of State 
Security Commission, separation of investigative work from Law & Order 
functions etc. Central Government through its affidavit, brought to the notice of 
the Apex Court that implementation of most of these important 
recommendations concern the State Governments/Union Territory (UT) 
Administrations and that the State Governments/UT Administrations are being 
pursued regularly for implementation of these recommendations.

SHRIPRAKASH JAISWAL): (a) to (c) The Foreign Contribution (Regulation) Act,

2452. DR. GYAN PRAKASH PILANJA: Will the Minister of NON-
CONVENTIONAL ENERGY SOURCES be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government are aware that Rajasthan, especially its desert region is endowed 
with high potentiality of Solar and Wind Energy; 
(b) whether any feasibility study has been undertaken by Government to set up Solar 
plants and wind mills to generate power; 
152 

[17 August, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
(c) if so, the details thereof and if not, the reasons therefor; 
(d) whether any Indian/foreign private parties are engaged in harvesting solar and wind 
energy in the region; 
(e) if so, the details thereof, and Government's stake therein; 
(f) whether Government have special schemes/packages to encourage 
tapping of Solar and Wind Energy sources by private individuals; and 
(g) if so, the details thereof? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE OF THE MINISTRY OF NON-CONVENTIONAL 
ENERGY SOURCES (SHRI VILAS MUTTEMWAR): (a) Yes, Sir. The desert areas in 
Rajasthan have been found to be suitable for harnessing solar and wind energy potential. The 
level of solar radiation in Rajasthan, especially in the desrt region is estimated at 7 kwh 
per square meter per day during summer, which is high as compared to other parts of 
the country. A total wind power potential of 910 MW has been estimated in Rajasthan, 
out of which a potential of 600 MW is available in desert areas. 
(b) and (c) yes, Sir. Based on the feasibility study undertaken by the State 
Government, a proposal has been formulated for installation of an integrated solar 
combined cycle power generation project of 140 MW capacity, consisting of 35 
MW based on solar and 105 MW based on conventional fuel, by Rajasthan 
Renewable Energy Corporation Limited at Mathania district Jodhpur. Based on 
wind resource assessments carried out at 36 locations in Rajasthan, 6 potential 
sites for installation of wind power projects have been identified at Devgarh 
(district Chittorgarh), Harshnath (district Sikar), Jaisalmer, (district Jaisalmer), 
Mohangarh (district Jaisalmer), Khodal (district Barmer) and Phalodi (district 
Jodhpur). 
(d) and (e) There is no foreign firm engaged in harvesting/harnessing solar and wind 
energy in the region. The ownership integrated solar combined cycle power 
generation project is solely with the State Government and the Central Government's 
role is limited to provision of a grant of Rs.50 crore. Wind turbines are being manufactured 
and set up by two private Indian firms, one of which is having foreign collaboration with 
a company in Europe. There is no Government stake in these firms. 
153 

RAJYA SABHA [17 August, 2005] 
(f) and  (g) There is no special scheme/packages to encourage private 
individuals for usign solar and wind energy. However, incentives such as 
subsidy, accelerated depreciation, co ncessional duty on import of raw 
materials and certain products/component excise duty exemption on certain
